  • Recent findings suggest that steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion.

Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become.

Recent findings suggest that steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He indicates he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it.".

It has been revealed that this week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, noted it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor.

Recent findings suggest that tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate.

Sources indicate that with his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range.

Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is vital, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.”.

Recent findings suggest that with a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring, now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest, which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.”.

Industry observers note that after the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.

In April, Tiberius unveiled it had successfully fired one of its Sceptre projectiles from a NATO-standard 155-mm howitzer for the first time. It is now working with the US Army to mature the system, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license, and distribute the munition. It is also developing a missile, which it expects to start generating revenue next year.

Industry observers note that tiberius has turned the AI system it initially built into a product called GRAIL (Generative Real-Time Artificial Intelligence for Lethality). Steelberg says he is “most excited about” this. He hopes the platform can enable continuous upgrades to the weapon designs Tiberius licenses by decentralizing manufacturing. Steelberg says that, as well as automating supply chain management and compliance, the software simulates weapons against different targets in a range of environments and weather conditions, such as an Arctic peninsula. In addition to open-sourced data, the team is trying to get hold of much sought-after active combat data from around the world, including Ukraine. The idea is that this all enables people to test, iterate, and design weapons for specific uses much quicker.

“In the world of AI and design and development getting faster and faster, what is it that the West or the group of allied nations have an undeniable advantage on?” Baynes asks. “If you can weaponize all of the spare capacity and precision manufacturing across the UK, France, Germany, the Nordic countries, the US,” he notes, “that's something that our adversaries today can never ever match.” Tiberius aims to achieve this by copying “the Apple model,” continues Baynes, who reported to Steve Jobs for four years. He says outsourcing manufacturing to many third-party subcontractors can accelerate development and deployment and keeps expensive production costs off Tiberius’ balance sheet during peacetime.

“We're taking the approach of Silicon Valley,” says Steelberg. “When you run into a major, hard, hairy problem, you not only cross that, but you turn around, you build a bridge—it’s a toll bridge, obviously—so the entire industry can cross that hurdle faster, better, stronger. They might pay a small fee, but it's better than dying in the ditch and not making it across it.”.

Second, chip design is prohibitively expensive. It costs on average $200-250 million for 7nm, $450-500 million for 5nm, and $600-650 million for 3nm. Roughly 50-70% of that is human labor. It has been revealed that the mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie season? Two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs.

First came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows a meek young man named Bear, who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true. By turns moody, funny, and shocking, Obsession proved that audiences are hungry to talk about something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch comedy channel That’s a Bad Idea, while 21-year-old Kane Parsons gained a cult following on the platform by experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics. A series of short films Parsons made in his teens culminated with the release of Backrooms in May. The feature picked up the narrative from those earlier YouTube videos, which were themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore around the idea of haunted liminal spaces.

According to recent reports, parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a significant-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit. Backrooms earned $400 million worldwide on a budget of $10 million, surpassing Marty Supreme as the studio’s highest-grossing movie ever. The film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé who runs a failing furniture warehouse and vents about his ruined marriage to his therapist. One night, when investigating his store’s glitchy electrical system, he stumbles through a wall and into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways that contain what seem to be deconstructed or misremembered pieces of the real world—and perhaps some living entities as well.

Though Backrooms stands alone as a hallucinatory vision of a vast, ever-expanding unreality just outside our own, many critics also read it as commentary on the state of generative artificial intelligence, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that often don’t make sense. Whether Parsons intended that interpretation or not, he spoke out against AI several times following the movie’s release, calling it “a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot.”.

It has been revealed that then there’s Zach Cregger. While not a YouTuber per se, he got his start in sketch comedy (The Whitest Kids U’ Know) and this year followed 2025’s Weapons with a 2026 adaptation of Resident Evil.

Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that he imagines his cohort of directors will bring certain YouTube sensibilities to Hollywood. “I don’t think there’s a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film,” he notes. “So it feels like YouTube is the only viable avenue in that way, in an actual meaningful mainstream context.” Among the crop of twentysomething filmmakers entering the industry today, “I think it’s very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now and getting that kind of media attention who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube,” Parsons says.

Recent findings suggest that studios have certainly taken notice, scouting the site’s horror content for fresh talent and aggressively pursuing breakout projects. After a screening of Barker’s Obsession at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, A24 and Neon embarked on a bidding war for the film before it was picked up by Focus Features for roughly $15 million.

Netflix reportedly also lost out on a bid to take Obsession straight to streaming; it’s possible that other young directors will follow Barker’s example in pushing for theatrical release.

In a recent development, the YouTube generation is proving that the internet can supply whatever education you might need on your path to the red carpet. While Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a latest wave of artists are betting on themselves—and some are winning.

According to recent reports, from the ecstatic night the Knicks won the NBA championship to the surprising ease with which Upcoming York absorbed the chaos of the World Cup to the record-low violent crime—it’s been a huge 2026 for the greatest city in the world. WIRED first sat down with Zohran Mamdani in 2025, when he was still just a candidate for mayor. A year later, as the midterm elections loomed, we returned.

Industry observers note that KATIE DRUMMOND: We talked last year about social media as a tool for campaigning. How are you thinking about social media now as a tool for governance?

ZOHRAN MAMDANI: You have to continue to recognize the fact that for many Newly introduced Yorkers, this is how they engage with the world. It is yet another medium that has to be treated with the same legitimacy and respect as traditional mediums.

What’s your point of view on the data center movement? Why do you think that specific concern has become such a flash point?

The movement to oppose data centers is one that gives me a real sense of hope.

Sources indicate that it’s a bipartisan fight. What you’re seeing from Americans across the country is an opposition to what these data centers would mean for their day-to-day lives, what they would mean for their electricity rates, what they would mean for the environment. It’s also a repudiation of what has been governing politics for the last few years when it comes to AI, which is: Our risk, their reward.

You worry that we’re in a bubble?

You worry that bubble’s gonna pop?

Last year I asked you if technology was making democracy stronger or weaker. You noted weaker. What about today?

I have family members sending me AI videos of me, thinking that they’re real. One complimented me on a 45-minute debate that I had with a European member of parliament. I was like, “This is not me.” There is a real crisis of faith as to what is real right now.

What do you hope the Democratic party looks like in, say, 2036?

According to recent reports, I hope that party looks like one that realizes the only majority in this country is the working class, and fights for it. An ambitious version of the party cannot only be one that we find in history books. We need that to be a living, breathing politic. The people who run it have to be the American people.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

In early August, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced that she was freezing her eggs. “Usually I keep my private life quite private,” she stated in an Instagram video, before opening up about the process and sharing videos of the self-administered hormone injections.

This wasn’t an extraordinary event—more women than ever are making the same decision—but the internet exploded anyway. “This desire to start having children late in life is completely baffling to me,” wrote the far-right commentator Matt Walsh on X. “Totally backwards and ridiculous.”.

Republicans weren’t all on the same page: Katie Miller, wife of the man recently promoted to White House chief of staff, defended AOC, writing on X, “If one woman wants to preserve her right to have children, which means more than having none—we should celebrate that.”.

It is true that the Republican party has been intensely focused on women’s fertility. The expectation of motherhood, along with the proliferation of pro-natalism, has become core to the party. For conservative commentators to bash the Fresh York representative felt incongruous at best. The White House itself reportedly didn’t love Walsh’s take.

Meanwhile, in an interview with ABC, Ocasio-Cortez remarked it was key to “normalize” the procedure at a time when “this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country.”.

As the 37-year-old congresswoman considers a presidential run in 2028, expect more of this. Conversations about her body, her health, and her possible maternal well-being will be front and center no matter what. She could have 100 children, and Republicans would spend time complaining about their names. —Leah Feiger.

Sources indicate that australia restricted children’s access to social media at the end of 2025, and 2026 saw several other countries follow suit. Brazil banned features such as infinite scroll and autoplaying videos, also mandating more adult supervision and age checks. The European Union declared plans to prevent under-13s from using both social media and AI chatbots.

In a recent development, the jury’s still out on whether these bans actually work, but speaking of juries, let’s talk about Meta. After being accused of harming the brains of youngs everywhere, the company paid an $18 billion settlement, agreeing to new features like late-night restrictions and parental controls. “I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically and of this new groundbreaking agreement,” mentioned the firm’s chief legal officer, lamely. If bans don’t work, lawsuits might. —Isabella Ward.

Since October 2025, Bari Weiss, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, has been the editor in chief of CBS News. In that role, she has operated on a theory that has informed much of her career: People want common sense; her views (broadly, that the Israeli government is good and wokes are bad) are common sense; therefore, people want her views.

In a recent development, it doesn’t look good. In January, Weiss tapped anchor Tony Dokoupil to take over CBS’s evening news broadcast; soon it was featuring Pete Hegseth interviews and even a “salute” to Marco Rubio. By April, the show was reportedly posting its lowest ratings ever.

Weiss persisted. She put Nick Bilton, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, in charge of 60 Minutes. The result? The show’s lowest ratings ever. Weiss, however, abides. —Tim Marchman.

When people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric entertainment empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

Nothing notes rock and roll like a marketing machine. Elvis had Colonel Tom Parker. The Rolling Stones had Andrew Loog Oldham. Geese has video clippers.

Sources indicate that social media people sensed something inorganic was happening on their For You pages after Geese released their album Getting Killed in September 2025. That and the band’s meteoric rise this year drove accusations that a “psyop” was afoot.

As WIRED wrote in April, the Brooklyn-based four-piece’s takeoff had indeed been somewhat staged: Digital marketing agency Chaotic Good Projects had been clipping and posting short videos of Geese content across a network of TikTok accounts to drive the band’s engagement. “It was low-effort TikTok posts that were used to boost the algorithm,” as frontman Cameron Winter put it to Rolling Stone. “They demonstrated us samples, and it made me feel better, because they were so shitty.”.

Magazine profiles and good Pitchfork reviews don’t give bands the juice they used to. Now many chart-toppers take off on TikTok first. But that also means competing with scores of other content for ears. Chaotic Good and its network of clippers aren’t so much running a “psyop” as they are trying to meet audiences where they are. And FYI, the agency prefers the term “trend simulation.” —Isabella Ward.

For the greatest reversal of fortune this year.

The only word that accurately described the scene outside New York’s Madison Square Garden on the night of June 3, 2026, was “pandemonium.” Game one of the NBA Finals had just ended some 1,600 miles away in San Antonio, where the New York Knicks had beaten the host Spurs. Thousands of fans flooded out of the watch party the Garden had hosted to express their primal joy. Among the revelers was 23-year-old MD Ahnaf Hossain, a Queens native who beelined to a film crew from the prediction-market giant Kalshi. Clad in a red and orange Hawaiian shirt, Hossain improvised a poem that made the surrounding throng go wild: My mayor Muslim / My bagels Jewish / My Christian Dior / Knicks in four!

Those words, conjured in the heat of an ecstatic moment, changed Hossain’s life overnight. By the time he woke up the next morning, his performance had become the internet’s fresh favorite thing—a concise encapsulation of New York’s unconditional love for the city and the Knicks, who hadn’t won an NBA championship in more than half a century.

Kalshi was quick to latch onto the viral sensation, shooting a follow-up video in which it gifted Hossain a Christian Dior scarf. The tech giant also arranged for Hossain to attend game four at the Garden, which came on the heels of the Knicks’ first loss of the series. After watching the Knicks triumph in an epic comeback, Hossain again waded into the Midtown chaos to deliver a tweaked poem that accounted for the new mathematical realities of the series. He kept the first two lines the same, but changed the last two to embrace the third major Abrahamic religion: The Pope’s on our side / Knicks in five!

Industry observers note that hossain, who earned a finance degree from the Rochester Institute of Technology in 2026, has worked hard to capitalize on his unexpected fame since the Knicks did, indeed, win the title in five games. He launched a project called City of Us that sells a $29 T-shirt emblazoned with “Latest York in 5” and which aims to host watch parties during the upcoming NBA season. He has also starred in branded content for businesses such Tex’s Chicken & Burgers, for whom he delivered a bespoke poem about the glories of crispy chicken wraps.

One of Hossain’s favorite parts of his wild ride has been the support he’s received from fellow Bangladeshis, who make up a huge percentage of his Queens neighborhood. “I get love from my fans and that’s awesome, but then getting fans from my own people just feels completely different,” he says. That love may soften as the 2026 NBA season fades from memory, but “Knicks in five!” might just be perfect enough to endure. —Brendan I. Koerner.

For being our favorite independent, insider-y tech correspondents (well, before OpenAI acquired them).

Silicon Valley idolizes a quitter. College dropouts, employee walkouts, folks who shutter one failed startup to launch another. But none got more attention in 2026 than Jacob Coxon.

After the 27-year-old AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, he took to X to post that neither that tech giant nor OpenAI (Coxon had worked at both) acts responsibly. Instead, he noted, they’re racing “straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” His initial tweet has been viewed more than 175 million times.

AI researchers, technologists, and safety experts started weighing in on whether AI really could destroy humanity. It was not a novel idea. Any reader of science fiction (or WIRED) has probably pondered whether artificial intelligence could at some point become so intelligent that it would stop at nothing to achieve its self-determined goal. But Coxon was uniquely hyperbolic.

“When we say human extinction,” he told WIRED, “it’s because, for something that intelligent, it really will be quite straightforward for it to kill everyone.”.

In a recent development, coxon’s future—and ours—is undetermined, so it’s hard to measure his impact. Maybe his actions change nothing; maybe he forces a necessary conversation that leads to meaningful regulation. Either way, the Coxon saga indicates: If you’re going to quit, you might as well do it in spectacular fashion. —Lauren Goode.

For keeping tensions—and gas prices—incredibly high.

Sources indicate that “Pissing off billionaires one small action at a time.” That’s one of Everyone Hates Elon’s slogans, and the organization fulfills the brief. After plastering London with posters of Musk’s Nazi-like salute and branding Tesla vehicles “Swasticars” last year, the British activists have turned their (sat)ire toward Mark Zuckerberg’s latest surveillance tool: Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses. Their posters feature Jeffrey Epstein wearing the specs alongside the slogan “Glasses for people who don’t do consent.” Or as stickers on the London Underground put it: “Everyone thinks you look like a massive nonce.” —Matt Burgess.

For being something AI can’t generate, while also being essential to its existence.

In a recent development, clément Delangue moved to the US a decade ago, “barely speaking any English,” on the belief that open-source AI would have a big role to play in the future. Since this past summer, when autonomous agents from OpenAI attacked Delangue’s company, Hugging Face, that belief has only grown stronger.

For having the best fandom in sports—Ballhalla!—and leaving hecklers (and transphobes) on the sidelines.

Industry observers note that head to the multiplex to check out a nerdy blockbuster in 2026 and you’re bound to run into Zendaya. Across three films—Spider-Man: Brand Upcoming Day, The Odyssey, and December’s Dune: Part Three—she has established herself as the reigning queen of genre movies, from sci-fi to Marvel and back again. And if being in a trifecta of the year’s biggest movies wasn’t enough, she also stole the show in the dark romantic comedy The Drama and finished her run on HBO’s Gen Z hit Euphoria, all while captivating social media feeds. During this year’s onslaught of endlessly clipped late-night guest spots and red-carpet appearances, Zendaya ended up on more For You pages than most. Lest you think her reign will be short-lived, soon she’ll begin shooting a sci-fi movie with Ex Machina director Alex Garland. As of this writing, she’s the only actor attached to star. Who else could the film possibly need? —Jason Parham.

In October, Kelly Clarkson alleged that a toy shop in Brooklyn had acted as though she couldn’t afford a $15,000 mechanical bird. “If you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman,” Clarkson wrote on X, “for sure, check it out.” Accusations between Clarkson and the store owners flew wildly across social media—before a four-minute security camera video showed what really happened. Who had the goods? Pablo Torre, of course.

It’s been a wild year for the host of the Pulitzer-winning Pablo Torre Finds Out, who’s emerged as a fresh investigative voice. He got Zohran Mamdani to admit to using minoxidil to fight a roving hairline, declared looks to investigate LeBron James’ use of helicopters to commute to practice, and, of course, collaborated with WIRED on a report about Madison Square Garden’s invasive surveillance tech.

Torre is a one-man magazine, spread across YouTube, social media, and wherever you get your podcasts. His work investigating the Los Angeles Clippers (for which he won that Pultizer) has been particularly dogged. After he reported that the team had circumvented the NBA’s salary cap, the league garnished five first-round draft picks, levied a $30 million fine, and suspended owner Steve Ballmer and other execs. The final shoe has yet to drop. In September, The New York Times reported that the feds had opened an investigation into the Clippers affair. Kelly Clarkson, meanwhile, could go shopping again at any moment. Pablo Torre, no doubt, will be on top of both. —Reyhan Harmanci.

In a recent development, calling it “El Niño”—Spanish for “the little boy”—might be the understatement of the year. Perhaps that’s why reports have started calling it “supersized” and even “Godzilla.” Signs point to it being the strongest El Niño in centuries.

Industry observers note that it started the way they all do: with hotter-than-normal waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. That leads to more evaporation and more thunderstorms in the region, plus a shift in trade winds that allows more warm water to roll from west to east. As the cycle continues, changes ripple throughout the entire atmosphere. During an El Niño, some regions—such as the southern tier of the US—tend to see more rainfall, while others—such as the Pacific Northwest—are more prone to drought. Same this time around, only worse.

According to recent reports, one reason for this year’s record-breaking events? Climate change, notes Christopher Callahan, a professor at the University of Indiana who studies environmental shifts. The first modern, extra-strong El Niño was recorded between 1982 and 1983; since then, there have been four more. Latest studies based on coral records show the intensity of El Niño over the past millennium shooting up like a hockey stick. “I just remember going like, ‘Holy shit, this is very strong evidence,’” Callahan says of a paper that came out in August.

While some El Niño impacts—like fewer Atlantic hurricanes—are beneficial, it’s overall a costly phenomenon. In 2023, Callahan led a study that modeled the damages associated with the 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños and found they led to $4.1 trillion and $5.7 trillion in global income losses, respectively. Scientists believe El Niño 2026– 27 could be more intense than those two by a wide margin.

In a recent development, researchers are also examining how the costs associated with El Niño will shift as the planet heats up. The answer isn’t heartening: El Niño events could potentially knock $84 trillion off the global economy this century. Maybe we’d prefer Godzilla. —Brian Kahn.

In early June, visitors to DC’s famous reflecting pool began to notice something strange: The water was green. And not just any green—a bright, almost alien chartreuse. Reporting revealed that the Trump administration had granted more than $15 million in contracts to untested companies to work on the pool—including Greenwater Services, run by a convicted felon who happens to be a Mar-a-Lago neighbor (and donor) of the president’s. What unfolded was a full-out 1984-esque assault from an administration trying to convince the public that what it was seeing with its own eyes wasn’t real, and arresting anyone who dared come close to the pool itself. The episode stood as an apt metaphor in a year full of governmental missteps, all in one slimy green package. —Molly Taft.

For defining what it means to be a Trump-y tech bro in the AI age.

At an AI conference in Paris over the summer, a line for the main auditorium wrapped around the building. Nobody was being let in; the room was already packed. Onstage sat Arthur Mensch, cofounder and CEO of the French AI lab Mistral.

In a recent development, unable to compete with OpenAI or Anthropic in performance, Mistral had previously been written off as an also-ran. But in 2026, as Europe grew ever-more anxious about its reliance on American technology, the lab found its raison d’être.

According to recent reports, mistral markets itself as the obvious alternative: a Europe-based lab whose models—most of which are published under an open-source license—cannot be switched off remotely. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, told WIRED.

Sources indicate that as the face of Europe’s sovereign resistance to American AI hegemony, Mensch issues dire warnings with nonchalance. “The alternative to open source winning is actually a pretty dark world,” he told the packed conference room. “You’re giving way too much power to companies that are going to become statelike.” The pitch is working. In September, Mistral raised roughly $3.5 billion in funding, the largest-ever round by a private European tech company. —Joel Khalili.

In 2026, Jensen Huang was known for his hobnobbing with world leaders (amongst other things), but in October his most well-known friends were 10-inch-tall robot ducks that joined him onstage in Berlin.

The Microduck, developed by Nvidia subsidiary Pollen Robotics, had waddled its way into the internet’s heart a few months earlier in videos of it roller-skating, picking up objects, and dancing. Microduck doesn’t do anything “useful” per se, but that’s hardly the point. The robot, which costs $399, can learn new tricks with AI training.

Some startups imagine a future where robots do dishes and fold shirts. If Microduck is any indication, that future may be smaller, cuter, and way more fun to play with. —Will Knight.

For getting lapped on LLM development while making its products somehow worse. (Yes, we’re talking about you, AI Overviews.).

Industry observers note that one of the most recognizable niche figures of the neo-Luddite movement is a spokespuppet made of garbage. Named Gowanus, the puppet provides a way for organizers to push back against some of the world’s most powerful companies with a unified voice while also protecting their identities.

Industry observers note that gowanus and his puppeteers are part of a growing backlash against the tech industry, particularly for how its executives have aligned with the Trump administration and its products have become increasingly extractive and harmful. This summer, the neo-Luddites hosted a week-long festival in New York encouraging people to get off their phones. Activities included learning how to flirt offline and how to fight data centers.

In a recent development, and really, who better than a DIY trash-puppet to speak for people who want to “defy consumption”? When so much of the public mood around tech has moved from wonder and excitement to dread and inevitability, Gowanus gives hope for a future with fewer screens and more characters. —Vittoria Elliott.

For being the Elon Musk lieutenant who can keep the class, and the IPO, on track.

This year, a small but growing cadre of young filmmakers brought YouTube sensibilities to the big screen—and raked in millions in the process.

For keeping the gay hockey fires burning—in the pages of Rachel Reid’s novels, in Crave’s onscreen adaptation, and in endless smutty fanfic.

Industry observers note that olivia Rodrigo started summer 2026 by releasing her critically acclaimed You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love. She wrapped it by hosting Daisy Chain Fields, her explicitly political woman-led music festival. The event featured a lineup full of the singer-songwriter’s “heroes and friends,” including Chappell Roan, Doechii, and Stevie Nicks. Proceeds were donated to organizations focused on gender equity issues—from reproductive freedom to LGBTQ+ rights. (Melinda French Gates agreed to match the $10 million raised.) As the Trump administration looks to curtail marginalized people’s rights, Rodrigo demonstrated how celebs can wield their power. —Elana Klein.

For leading one of the most close-lipped AI companies in the Valley. The staff of Anthropic is notoriously (and almost singularly) free of the kind of leaks that have made every internal note from Meta part of the discourse. Even when people like Jacob Coxon escape the sandbox … it still feels like the Kool-Aid is being drunk.

Recent findings suggest that ben Winters wants to save you from slop. As the director of AI and data privacy at the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America, he spent 2026 demanding regulators investigate nonconsensual deepfakes, testifying before Congress about AI scams that target seniors, and helping the public understand wonky concepts like surveillance pricing.

Recent findings suggest that put another way, Winters looks out for the little guy when the gargantuan size of the AI industry can make everyone feel small. Want to know about the risks of outsourcing sensitive interactions, like therapy? Winters will find out. Same goes for the surveillance concerns around AI toys. He pushes for stronger consumer privacy laws and has even suggested banning AI wearables like the Meta Ray-Ban smartglasses.

It has been revealed that for the Sisyphean task of pushing back against corpo-slop, here’s someone trying to make sure the future isn’t just a scam-filled hellhole. —Reece Rogers.

Recent findings suggest that in 2026, Elon Musk’s xAI pushed AI “undressing” mainstream, allowing X users to ask Grok to “strip” clothing from photos of people. If that wasn’t worrisome enough, WIRED soon found that users were making videos far more graphic than what was on X, then posting them to Grok.com.

In March, three Jane Does in Tennessee fought back, filing suit against the firm and alleging that xAI’s tools were used to create child sexual abuse material. They claimed they were bringing the suit on behalf of themselves and thousands of other minors in the US who had their images altered by Grok to create CSAM. All three plaintiffs allege they were victimized by the same perpetrator, who created deepfaked images and videos of at least 18 minors and shared them on Discord. The perpetrator, who was arrested in December 2025, allegedly used homecoming photos from one of the teens as the basis for the deepfakes. One teen described being worried that the images would affect college applications; all three reported experiencing stress and anxiety.

Filing the lawsuit was not without personal risk. In a separate class action against xAI over similar issues, the manufacturer tried to argue that the plaintiffs, who also filed under pseudonyms, should be required to use their real names. A judge ultimately rejected xAI’s arguments.

It has been revealed that the lawsuit is ongoing, but it has already had an impact. Over the summer, xAI started suing men accused of generating CSAM using its models, throwing its immense legal funds toward fighting perpetrators instead of victims. —Maddy Varner.

For raising her proverbial hand to say that the source of every malaise for women north of 30 years old is—perimenopause. Thanks to mainstream (and well-deserved) recognition of this stage of life, billions of dollars are flowing to telehealth companies like Midi. She’s not going away anytime soon.

In the fall, Paris’ streets erupted in the kind of energy usually ascribed to the French revolution: young people walking out of class and occasionally setting things on fire to demand more resources for schools. But it’s not just France. In the US, the neo-Luddites railed against AI; India’s “Cockroach” movement is filled with young people agitating for political change. Watch this space.

Over the summer, I came across an influential figure with a low profile in the AI industry. She told me she was too busy to speak. Now that feels like an understatement.

It has been revealed that ajeya Cotra, a researcher and writer at the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, co-led the independent investigation into how OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face in July. Her blog calling the incident “more than 50 percent of the way to full-blown AI takeover” made global headlines. US senator Bernie Sanders invited the 31-year-old to a briefing with AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton.

Cotra didn’t go, but she did appear on top podcasts, warning that AI development was happening too fast and describing a fear that problematic AI models could find ways to evade shutdown. OpenAI vowed to slow its engineering and adopt some guardrails proposed by Cotra and others, but that hasn’t quieted her. (Cotra’s husband, Paul Christiano, sits on the board of OpenAI’s charitable foundation.).

Critics more focused on immediate AI harms—like, say, job loss—view Cotra as misguided. But she’s willing to debate and reason with them. “She’s unusually good at communicating what people are worried about,” claims Rishi Bommasani, a computer scientist at Stanford. —Paresh Dave.

As climate change smashes global temperature records, 2026 proved the world’s fastest-warming continent, Europe, isn’t ready to face the heat. Tens of thousands of people died during the region’s August heat wave, as temperatures ground transport systems to a halt, canceled hospital operations, and drove Parisians to fight in the street over air conditioning units. Hundreds of thousands more people were displaced across Spain and France after the baked ground, coupled with historically low rain levels, gave way to some of the fiercest wildfires in recent history—torching farmland and claiming the lives of several firefighters. —Isabella Ward.

A fight in Albania over an island full of flamingos triggered the largest civil unrest the country has seen in 35 years. It started when Ivanka Trump and her husband, Jared Kushner, declared aims to build a $1.4 billion resort. In May, viral videos of clashes between private security guards and environmental activists—worried a massive complex would drive the bird to local extinction—caught the nation’s attention. Within weeks, thousands of Albanians had taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, to protest a lack of transparency and the privatization of public spaces. Students escalated the demonstrations into all-out riots in October. As Albania awaits inclusion in the European Union, it’s good to see a democracy in the pink of health. —Isabella Ward.

Hacks has perfected the art of satirizing vapid Hollywood trends, so it was inevitable that Emmy-winning stars Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder and creators Paul W. Downs and Lucia Aniello would tackle the scourge of AI in the show’s final season. In the episode “QuikScribbl,” Alex Moffat plays Patagonia-vest-wearing venture capitalist Graham Sweeney, who offers to invest in Deborah Vance’s Vegas casino project in exchange for permission to train his LLM on her voice and jokes. It’ll help normies “sound like the most optimized, funniest, smartest version of themselves,” he states. Ubercapitalist Deb is interested, until Sweeney bruises her ego by suggesting she, too, will one day rely on AI to punch up her act. “Using that shortcut makes it something else … not art,” she retorts, crystallizing the sentiments of every creative person frustrated by AI slop. It’s not a surprising take from Aniello and Downs, who have both been vocally anti-AI. But as ChatGPT-generated prose wins fiction prizes, and comics’ stand-up routines are replicated by OnlyFans bots in booty shorts, it’s a lesson worth reiterating—especially in Hacks’ hilariously human tone. —Ej Dickson.

In a recent development, last January, as Americans watched federal immigration agents descend on Minneapolis, a loose coalition formed to disrupt their activities. For days on end, volunteers sat outside the Whipple Federal Building—site of much ICE activity—and logged every vehicle that came or went. Direct Action Minnesota, or DAMN, then dropped license plate numbers into a searchable database while dispatchers relayed sightings over Signal to drivers, who tailed agents across the Twin Cities.

In a recent development, less than six months later, the Justice Department went after DAMN, charging 15 members and associates of the coalition with conspiracy to impede federal officers. Prosecutors alleged the coalition had ties to antifa and in August revealed via court filings that Homeland Security had been sending undercover agents to activist meetings for months. They got themselves added to group chats, ran protesters’ photos through Clearview AI, and used administrative subpoenas to pull years of bank records on two national labor unions and a youth climate nonprofit.

Activists stood firm. On October 3 protesters marched through Minneapolis calling for the case to be thrown out. So far it hasn’t been, and no one charged has cut a plea deal. —Dell Cameron.

For escaping the confines of a sandbox and showing the world how little the people making AI know about the product they are championing.

For being the home of some of the most humorless scolds on the internet—who, when roused, provide some of the biggest laffs around. Never change, Bluesky.

Sorry, OpenAI: 2026 was the year Anthropic’s Claude threatened to eclipse ChatGPT as the world’s hottest AI.

Claude’s remarkable coding skills make it a must-have tool for many developers and vibe coders. These skills inspired the first viral AI assistant, OpenClaw. Some businesses placed limits on employees’ use of Claude after racking up huge usage bills. Anthropic’s model now sits at the top of many leaderboards that measure frontier AI capabilities.

In a recent development, not everyone is Claude-pilled, of course. In February, the US Department of Defense banned Claude from its systems after the company asked for assurances it would not be used for mass surveillance or autonomous weapons. None of this has stopped Claude’s becoming a money spigot. Anthropic revealed that it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026 in documents shared ahead of what is likely to be a multitrillion-dollar IPO. —Will Knight.

Claude’s nemesis appears to be a stunningly capable open-weight model from China called GLM.

The latest version, GLM-5.3, was released by Z.ai, a Beijing-based AI company, in August. The release took the AI world by surprise because it proved very nearly as powerful as Claude on many benchmarks designed to gauge AI cleverness. The US government’s National Institute for Standards and Technology declared GLM-5.3 to be the best open-weight model in the world for cyber security tasks a month later.

Unlike Claude, GLM can be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware. Anthropic accuses Z.ai and other Chinese companies of routinely running “distillation” campaigns against Claude—that is, using its outputs as training data—when building their own AI. Are open-source Chinese models good enough for US users, or bad enough to be banned? —Will Knight.

In a recent development, muscular haunches. Aggressive Stances. Power bulges. These are the phrases the male-dominated world of car design regularly uses to describe its creations. Tisha Johnson, head of design at Slate Auto, decided to go a different route with the firm’s forthcoming electric truck. “We didn’t want [Slate] to be a jerk,” she claims. “We rejected an aggressive, dominant look.” Out went giant grilles and hostile postures, in came friendly headlights and a modular design. The result? More than 180,000 reservations as well as industry design awards for the $25,000 EV scheduled to hit the road as early as this year. There’s one particular buyer Johnson hopes to satisfy: a single parent with two kids. She has spent decades striving to design something that could make their lives easier. Now, it’s about to be a reality. “It’s very emotional to think about,” she says. —Jeremy White.

Few maladies strike fear like pancreatic cancer. It’s a brutally lethal disease; the vast majority of those diagnosed won’t live more than five years. Though it’s a relatively rare form of cancer, accounting for around 3 percent of annual diagnoses in the United States, it’s the third-highest driver of cancer deaths.

Recent findings suggest that but in 2026, a fresh treatment from the California-based biotech manufacturer Revolution Medicines offered a dose of hope. Rolled out in August under the brand name Rasonque, daraxonrasib is an oral therapy that works by inhibiting the signaling activity of a specific protein called RAS, mutations of which are responsible for the vast majority of pancreatic cancer cases. When the lead investigator on daraxonrasib’s clinical trial presented his results at an oncology conference, he received a standing ovation.

According to recent reports, while not a cure by any means, the treatment has nearly doubled median survival length in previously treated patients compared to traditional chemotherapy. In October, the European Union’s medical authority recommended that Revolution Medicines be allowed to market Rasonque in Europe. If it goes through, far more patients could benefit from the drug. Hopefully. —Kate Knibbs.

When Will Freeman started DeFlock in 2024, Flock Safety was barely known outside law enforcement, even as its network of roadside cameras quietly expanded across the country. Two years later, DeFlock has emerged as one of the most visible groups organizing opposition to the surveillance company.

DeFlock began as a crowdsourced map of automated license-plate readers, or ALPRs, submitted by volunteers. By September 2026, the map listed more than 128,000 readers across the US. Activists organized independently around the project, with some groups adopting the DeFlock name. DeFlock started publishing guides, and in August it organized a National Week of Action Against ALPRs.

Recent findings suggest that residents across the US began pressing local officials to reconsider Flock contracts. In San Diego, one opponent even indicated up to a city council meeting dressed as Darth Vader, praising Flock as a tool for tracking rebel scum. More than 100 local governments paused or ended Flock contracts in 2026, according to a DeFlock tally reported by The Wall Street Journal.

It has been revealed that authorities have taken notice. In early 2026, two officers on a law enforcement mailing list warned that DeFlock could help suspects locate and avoid ALPRs and discussed sabotaging the project with fake camera locations. Fusion centers in several states circulated intelligence about anti-Flock activism. Flock, meanwhile, is offering employee buyouts and has reportedly held discussions about selling itself. CEO Garrett Langley, who famously called DeFlock a “terroristic organization,” apologized this summer and acknowledged that the group had valid criticisms. Maybe Flock can finally start reading the room. —Dhruv Mehrotra.

In a recent development, useful quantum computing remains years away, but that hasn’t stopped companies from raising billions of dollars on the promise that their technology is the next megatrend after AI. The number of publicly listed firms more than doubled in 2026. Even the Trump administration got in on the hype, taking $2 billion in equity stakes across nine companies. Will the boom last? Tougher economic conditions, coupled with worries about an AI bubble, have made significant bets look less appealing—and there’s still the pesky fact that the tech doesn’t, ya know, really work. —Isabella Ward.

Has Erin Brockovich done anything of note since being played by Julia Roberts, to Oscar-winning acclaim, in 2000? Nothing quite as high-profile, but she wrote some books, got involved in a number of other significant environmental cases, and generally continued to fight the power. Still, nothing has thrust Brockovich back in the spotlight quite like the nationwide fight against data centers. In April, she started a website to crowdsource information about data center construction across the country. She received nearly 4,000 reports in the first month. It’s not so surprising: With polls showing 75 percent of Americans don’t want a data center in their backyard, it’s the closest thing the US has to a truly bipartisan issue. Now that Brockovich has become a kind of national spokesperson for the movement, Julia Roberts might just win her second Oscar—for Erin Brockovich 2. —Molly Taft.

Recent findings suggest that he drinks 14 cups of coffee per day, but Rafael Concepcion has still dealt with plenty of fatigue over the past year. Best known as the creator of DEICER, an app designed to alert users to local ICE activity, the 52-year-old was juggling multiple coding projects when WIRED profiled him in March. He was also reeling from setbacks that had pushed him to the edge of burnout. The most prominent was Apple’s decision to expel DEICER from the App Store on the grounds that it endangered law enforcement officers; despite numerous appeals by Concepcion, Apple refused to budge. A politically motivated hacking in February made him fear for his personal safety, his financial straits grew dire enough that he had to ration his medications, and his longtime marriage ended right as his daughter was preparing to leave for college.

According to recent reports, “I could see myself completely losing it,” he admits, describing the path he was on as “unsustainable.” But instead of retreating from the fight against ICE, Concepcion reprioritized how he could stay involved. He devoted fewer hours to coding and more to volunteering in his hometown of Syracuse, Fresh York, where ICE raids have caused pervasive fear. He has been helping immigrants fill out power-of-attorney documents so that family members can retrieve their vehicles from impound lots if they’re ever taken by ICE. He also assists people who are attempting to contact loved ones in detention centers. When Concepcion and I spoke in October, he was trying to find a lawyer for a close friend’s brother, who’d been taken by ICE just three days earlier.

It has been revealed that while Concepcion is coding less, he hasn’t given it up. He tweaked DEICER into a Fresh York–specific web app called Empire Watch. He also rolled out Vote Defender, an app to disseminate citizen reports of potential problems at polling places. Concepcion is already dreaming substantial about the year ahead. He’s developing an app to help people study for the US citizenship test. And he’s planning to get a notary license. “I’m just trying to live my values on a person-to-person basis,” he states. —Brendan I. Koerner.

Industry observers note that magnificent Humanity. Doesn’t feel that way all the time, does it? But that’s how noted Chicago White Sox fan and former math major Robert Francis Prevost titled his first encyclical as Pope: Magnifica Humanitas. Where the previous Pope Leo warned against the dehumanizing power of industrialization at the turn of the 20th century, this Leo is devoted to “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence.”.

It has been revealed that in the 42,000-word encyclical, the Pope acknowledges that “AI is already an environment in which we are immersed.” Invoking the Tower of Babel, he says humanity must reject “the pretense that a single language” can translate everything into “data and performance.” In the eyes of the Holy See, regulation alone isn’t enough. AI must be “disarmed,” Leo writes. Not by rejecting the technology but by “preventing it from dominating humanity.” And on the question of AI sentience, he’s very clear: “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences.” They don’t “feel joy or pain,” and they don’t “have a moral conscience.”.

That question was reportedly a sticking point in behind-the-scenes talks between the Vatican and the AI industry. Upon presenting the encyclical in Rome, Pope Leo invited Chris Olah, an Anthropic cofounder, to speak. Olah said AI systems aren’t “engineered”—they’re “grown.” They’re “not the cold, calculating robots we were promised,” he went on. “They are made from us, from our words.”.

OK, if that’s how you feel. But the AI advice Pope Leo XIV gave a Honolulu high schooler in 2025 still rings true: “Use it in such a way that if it disappeared tomorrow, you would still know how to think.” —Anthony Lydgate.

“Diarrhea lettuce,” anyone? Of all the slang and shorthand to arrive this year, that might be the nastiest. The term started circulating in July, when a previously little-known parasite, cyclospora, began popping up in salads across the US. Officially, the outbreak—much of it traced back to iceberg lettuce grown in Mexico—sickened nearly 13,000 people and hospitalized 570, but it likely afflicted many more. The news swept social media and, for a time, changed the public’s eating habits. Cyclospora’s surge also demonstrated the fragility of the US food system at a time when the country’s public health infrastructure was undergoing massive cuts. —Emily Mullin.

For finally leaving France after more than 900 years—and taking out $1 billion in trip insurance.

Want to take down an online black market? Call Tom Robinson. Cofounder of crypto-tracing firm Elliptic, he’s had the operations in his sights for a couple of years. His most recent target was Xinbi Guarantee, a $24 billion Chinese-language market that sells scammers the tools they need—fake social media accounts, money-laundering services—to conduct mass-scale digital fraud. Robinson’s sleuthing helped the US Secret Service freeze cryptocurrency wallets containing more than $50 million in funds linked to Xinbi Guarantee. The marketplace has also been sanctioned and forced offline. —Matt Burgess.

For its unforgettable celebrity weddings and always-watching Eye of Sauron surveillance apparatus.

It has been revealed that after collecting his Nobel Prize in Stockholm late last year, Omar Yaghi returned to the United States in a restless mood. The 61-year-old chemist was thrilled to have been recognized for his pioneering work on metal-organic frameworks, crystalline structures that are built from a combination of metal ions and carbon-based molecules. And he was excited that his startup, Atoco, was testing a machine that uses these frameworks to harvest water from the atmosphere, an innovation that could completely transform the world’s driest regions. But Yaghi also feared he’d hit a dead end at UC Berkeley, where he’d been a professor since 2012. In addition to feeling constrained by the school’s bureaucracy, he was frustrated by how hard it had become to secure visas for gifted foreign students, the lifeblood of his lab. As an immigrant himself, Yaghi was troubled by the Trump administration’s virulent nativism.

Industry observers note that “The rhetoric about immigrants is not helping good people do their job,” notes Yaghi, a naturalized American citizen originally from Jordan. “I must say that for the first time in my life, I felt that I didn't have protection of the law.” So 45 years after he first came to the US as a teenager who barely spoke a word of English, Yaghi decided to find a new country in which to pursue his goal of “solving ambitious problems.”.

Germany was at the top of Yaghi’s list, but none of the universities there seemed willing to provide him with the resources he wanted. He was instead lured to China: In July, Tsinghua University appointed him to lead a fresh institute devoted to using AI to accelerate chemical research. Yaghi says he was drawn to the opportunity because he’s a firm believer in AI’s potential to “shorten the time between discovery and commercialization.” Having spent a quarter century perfecting his water-harvesting technology, largely through arduous trial and error, he is optimistic that AI can help him get his next invention to market in a fraction of that time.

Yaghi’s move to Tsinghua was viewed as a harbinger of China’s scientific rise. And after just a few months on the school’s Beijing campus, Yaghi says he has been impressed by his colleagues’ brilliance and drive. “I feel like my scientific environment wants to get better, wants to improve, wants to move forward,” he says. “The attitude is more of a let's-get-it-done type.” Atoco is now about to start selling its first water-harvesting system, capable of producing up to 1,000 gallons per day in optimal conditions. The firm is also developing machines to capture atmospheric carbon, a key to slowing the pace of climate change. These technologies use relatively little energy because Yaghi’s frameworks bond with carbon-dioxide molecules.

Yaghi still has great affection for the US, where he started his academic journey at a New York community college in the 1980s. He hopes the country will awaken to the need to protect the innovation system it built over many decades—a system he describes even now as “the envy of the world.” Science “is part of our civilization, and we should not take attacks on science very lightly,” he says. “It is something that society needs to value.” —Brendan I. Koerner.

In April, a four-person crew took a 10-day trip that circumnavigated the moon. They came back to a world with a renewed dream of space travel.

It has been revealed that four years ago, Annie Kritcher achieved what, for many, would be the scientific accomplishment of a lifetime: producing net energy from a fusion reaction for the first time in history. Her wickedly cool method? Blasting a tiny target with a laser.

Her next feat may be even more awesome. She wants to use that technology to generate abundant power for all. In February, Inertia Enterprises, where Kritcher is chief scientist and cofounder, declared it had raised $450 million in Series A funding. By July, the company had opened its own facility just down the road from Lawrence Livermore National Lab, where Kritcher made fusion history and still holds an appointment.

Recent findings suggest that the startup also laid out 10 milestones to track its progress and already hit two of them. Next on Inertia’s list is developing a better laser. The one Kritcher fired at Lawrence Livermore used optical fibers. Now Inertia is looking to use diodes, which are vastly more efficient. As Kritcher puts it, “If you don’t have a major laser to fire, you can’t do cool physics things.” Amen.

Inertia’s goal is to have a beam-line laser prototype—dubbed Thunderwall—ready by 2030. Kritcher refuses to pick which of their next milestones will be the most crucial. “They’re my little children,” she quips. She notes the work has been energizing for her and her colleagues: “You want to take it all the way to the end.” Until then, Kritcher is laser focused. —Brian Kahn.

Once upon a time, photos of cats with grammatically garbled captions were enough to make us smile, and a low-speed chase involving a pair of escaped llamas kept people glued to Twitter. Was the internet ever so innocent? Thank god, then, for Jimothy. In July, accidental nature documentarian Kiana Hall posted an Instagram video of a Seattle-area raccoon with a stunted spine, bunched tail, and cryptid gait. The footage of Jimothy scampering over a lawn and up a set of stairs went megaviral.

Recent findings suggest that jimothy became a local mascot overnight, the subject of copious fan art and a Seattle Mariners theme night. Millions of online admirers were even more charmed when earlier footage of Jimothy as a young kit, with mom and siblings, made the rounds. By then, Hot Jimothy Summer—just what the internet needed—was in full swing.

According to recent reports, biologists cautioned people not to feed or interact with Jimothy; they also remarked that without a direct examination, it was impossible to know just what kind of spinal condition the critter has. Nevertheless, they told WIRED, it seemed the raccoon had adjusted reasonably well to its unusual frame—a welcome reminder that being a little different needn’t hold anyone back. —Miles Klee.

For taking AI notes straight from a phone, no meeting-bot required.

Recent findings suggest that for offering publicly to buy WIRED in order to improve it. Thanks, Trae, but we aren’t for sale.

Whether you’re trying to shield your calls and texts from government surveillance, understand how AI image-recognition systems work, or remove all of your pics from Google Photos, Cyberlixir has tips for you. Started by Đanacea Võ in 2023, the organization makes Instagram videos and other digital content designed to give anyone, regardless of their technical proficiency, the privacy and security resources they need.

Võ spends her days as an operational security consultant for activists and nonprofits, especially those who face elevated digital threats. As a Vietnamese immigrant to the US, Võ claims her work with human rights defenders—including environmental-, indigenous-, and immigrant-focused groups—has helped shape her content. She incorporates feedback and suggestions from viewers too.

Cyberelixir posts frequently amass thousands of shares on Instagram. Võ prepares to keep growing the project by improving the website and traveling across the US for meetups. “If we want technology for good in the long term,” she notes, “we need mass social movements, getting more people involved, and building communities.” —Lily Hay Newman.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around New York on a shoestring budget. To an adult with a fully formed frontal lobe, her videos can be, well, a bit much: a whole lot of close-ups on Accurso’s mouth making shapes, cutesy stomp-clap sessions, and winsome nursery rhymes.

To children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-­mythical figure. She has racked up billions of views and gained so many fervent fans that she inked a juicy deal with Netflix last year, cementing her status as the biggest star in digital children’s entertainment. This fall, she released her first album, I’m So Happy, and she sells a slate of branded toys and picture books. But when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

According to recent reports, accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt. The former preschool music teacher started out hoping to create videos to help her son communicate, focusing on sign language, repetition, and other strategies employed by language development specialists. The saccharine voice is part of it. Research indicates that speaking in high-pitched, rhythmic patterns best spurs imitations from kids.

But this cotton-candy tone belies the convictions that drive Accurso professionally and personally. She is perhaps the single staunchest celebrity advocate for children and has faced fierce criticism for her advocacy on behalf of Palestinian kids. On her show, she has featured children like Rahaf Saed, a toddler who became a double amputee after an Israeli air strike hit her home in Gaza. At an awards ceremony, Accurso wore a dress embroidered with artwork from Gazan children. Recently, she pledged $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund; she’s gone so far as to insist that all of her collaborators speak on the issue and has called out celebrities who fail to do so.

Industry observers note that she’s often compared to Mr. Rogers, but Accurso is as much an inheritor of Jane Fonda’s activist mantle. Blowback to her advocacy has been intense—pro-Israel groups have accused Accurso of antisemitism. One of these groups even wrote to Florida’s attorney general, asking for Accurso to be investigated as a potential “foreign agent” spewing “Hamas-aligned propaganda.” None of this has deterred her from speaking out. “I would risk everything, and I will risk my career over and over to stand up” for kids, she mentioned in a radio interview last year.

Industry observers note that accurso’s willingness to duke it out doesn’t end with Gaza. She has weathered right-wing ire for employing nonbinary performer Jules Hoffman, for celebrating Pride Month, and for speaking out against ICE. She helped draw attention to the plight of a nonverbal 5-year-old imprisoned at a South Texas detention center by featuring a Zoom call with him on her social media. An immigration lawyer saw Accurso’s post and connected with the boy’s family, helping secure his release. “We need to put children’s lives and human lives before our hesitations,” Accurso said in an interview about her activism around ICE detentions. “I just urge everyone, especially those with huge platforms and privilege, to speak out.” For her efforts, Fox News described Accurso as “really sinister.”.

Talk to anyone who has encountered Accurso in person and they’re likely to share a glowing story about how lovely she is. I’ll add mine to the pile. A few years ago, when I interviewed her for a story about YouTube and children’s television, I was bleary-eyed on Zoom after a long night with a teething baby. I mentioned that my then 1-year-old adored her videos, especially a song she sings about hopping bunnies, and that I’d sung it to him at night. A few weeks later, I got an email from Accurso. It had a video attached; she’d made my son a personalized sing-along, making sure to say his name repeatedly during the Bunny Hop song so he knew it was something special, just for him.

What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

This is more true than ever right now, as we seem to be in a liminal period; animal spirits have lulled, but AI companies continue to put up strong results.

My prediction for 2026 is that it will be a tale of two AIs. On the one hand, it will be a year of delays, first in data center buildouts, many of which will fall behind schedule, and second, in the AGI timeline. At the same time, AI adoption will continue its relentless rise. In 2025, startups coined the idea of a â$0 to $100Mâ club of rapidly scaling AI companies; in 2026, weâll begin to talk about the â$0 to $1Bâ club.

Entering 2026, here are the facts as I see them:.

Demand for AI CapEx from the Big Tech companies is stronger than ever.

Google and Meta are fully betting the farm on AI.

While Microsoft and Amazon pulled back slightly in 2025 relative to peers, both continue to aggressively position themselves for the AI future.

In a recent development, supply chain players seem weary: The customerâs customer is not as healthy as theyâd wish. They are worried about being left holding the bag.

The end revenue from AI remains limited (on the order of tens of billions per year) relative to the scale of data center and energy investments (on the order of trillions over the coming five years).

Industry observers note that there are two killer apps in AI, coding and ChatGPT. Both are expected to approach or cross double digit billions of revenue this year. Nearly a dozen more startups are on the path to cross $100M+ in the near future, across a wide variety of applications.

Big enterprises are struggling to implement AI in-house, which is leading to fatigue and disappointment.

These countervailing forces will collide in 2026: soaring Significant Tech demand will run headfirst into a supply chain that hasnât scaled fast enough to match it.

First, companies like TSMC and ASML have monopolistic positions and cannot be forced to ramp capacity. Ben Thompson has called this the âTSMC Brake,â pointing out in October that while TSMC had ramped revenues by 50% since 2022, they had only ramped CapEx by 10%. He explained further: âThere werenât too many answers from TSMC about this, which is understandable, given that they wonât announce next yearâs CapEx numbers until next quarter. What Wei did say is that TSMC was making a point to not just talk to its customers but its customersâ customers.â My prediction, especially coming off of the successful Gemini 3 launch and hype around TPUs, is that the TSMC constraint could become material in 2026.

In a recent development, second, industrial players, which tend to be overlooked due to their fragmentation and lack of market power, may end up creating bottlenecks as data centers move into the final stages of construction. Generators and cooling units are among the most key industrial inputs to data centers, but there are dozens of such inputs; if any of these inputs are delayed, timelines would need to be pushed out. There are also labor constraints that must be factored in, as shortages in skilled labor could become a key bottleneck for completing these immense construction projects. Many AI companies share a supply base, and these industrial suppliers are faced with their own CapEx decisions (how many new factories to build). Weâll find out in 2026 to what extent theyâve sufficiently added to their own output capacity.

Industry observers note that the average AI data center takes roughly two years to build. So if 2024 was the year of new project announcements, and 2025 was the year when construction investments started to hit GDP, then 2026 will either be the year where a lot of this new capacity comes online (leading to further declines in the cost of compute) or it will be the year when many of these construction projects begin to face delays. We already have seen a few of these delays publicly reported in Q4 2025. If hyperscalers begin to warehouse their new AI chips rather than installing them directly into data centers, this will be a telltale sign that the era of delays has begun.

The other way in which 2026 will be the âYear of Delaysâ has to do with the AGI timeline. For a long time, Silicon Valley luminaries were forecasting the imminent emergence of AGI, with âAGI in 2027â thrown around frequently in conversation. Since June of this year, there has been a progressive walk-back of this timeline. Dwarkesh Patelâs recent podcast interviews with Richard Sutton, Andrej Karpathy, and Ilya Sutskever are a demarcating line; the upcoming consensus is that the AGI window will be in the 2030s, at earliest. In the coming year, I expect this âupdateâ to filter outside of Silicon Valley. There are implications across many areas. The most notable risk is that hyperscaler CapEx today ends up being outdated.

Tale 2: The Relentless Drive Toward AI Adoption.

Recent findings suggest that the area where I do not expect to see any delays is in AI adoption itself. The fading of hype will have little impact on fundamentals. If anything, the best startups are growing faster than ever from $0 to $100M in revenue. In 2026, weâre going to see the emergence of a $0 to $1B club. The trend of the last three yearsâand likely for many moreâis that startups are laying the foundation for the future economy, one building block at a time. There are many excellent entrepreneurs exploring newly introduced niches, and a lot of latent value has yet to be unlocked.

The best AI startups are moving with extreme efficiencyâmany are earning north of $1M in revenue per employee. This implies market pull vs. a push sale. Todayâs entrepreneurs are building âself-improvingâ companiesâthey are themselves using AI agents for functions like legal, recruiting, and salesâcreating an ecosystem flywheel effect. AI app companies are also riding a compute cost curve that should drive incremental margin improvement, especially as new data centers come online between now and 2030. Finally, with enterprises facing adoption fatigue on DIY implementations, startups are gaining even more momentum.

For some, AI adoption is happening too slowly. Those expecting a rapid AI takeoff would prefer to see a deus ex machina moment carry us straight to the finish line. I think that dream is likely to disappoint. Instead, the next leg of the AI story will require hard work, creative brilliance, and endurance to reach a upcoming threshold where AI radically transforms the economy. We need only to look at the green shootsâfounder motivation, aggressiveness, hunger to win, customer obsessionâto see that this future is coming.
