📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of schedule, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.

“So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this tech giant and you do not worry about your comp,” she remarked.

In a recent development, questions about compensation were the most common among the 700 submitted ahead of the meeting, Kress said. She said the next-most common request was for transparency from the board.

Kress’ comments came during the first companywide meeting following the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO last week. Huang had led the computer graphics chip maker since cofounding it 33 years ago, and his presentations during the quarterly town halls internally had become a much-anticipated and memorable spectacle for some of the company’s nearly 49,000 employees. Information rarely leaked from the meetings in the past.

Recent findings suggest that but now Nvidia is facing an extraordinary leadership crisis. Huang resigned amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including potentially with a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday that Huang disclosed “personal behavior” contrary to the tech giant’s policies and norms and wouldn’t be invited back.

During the companywide meeting on Wednesday, Jones reiterated the board accepted Huang’s resignation due to his personal conduct and “lack of candor.” He noted the organization wouldn’t find a “Jensen clone,” but that there are “dynamic leaders out there, with demonstrated intellect, high tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility, and a track record of success.” He added, “We will not compromise our requirements for the sake of expediency” and that the board would accept employee suggestions on the CEO search.

It has been revealed that thousands of employees have apparently lobbied for Huang’s reinstatement. Several well-known tech executives signed a public petition, with about 200,000 purported backers urging the same. Instead, the board is searching internally and externally for a replacement at one of the world’s most valuable companies and one of the biggest drivers of the generative AI boom.

Huang’s departures and a slew of government investigations into him and Nvidia have rattled investors. But on Tuesday, Nvidia reported better than expected financial results and forecast growing sales in the years to come. Shares were up about 5 percent on Wednesday.

One concern investors have expressed is whether Nvidia might see a brain drain of top talent. Many employees have stayed at Nvidia for Huang and his vision. Nvidia could also be perceived as a less desirable place for new and emerging talent to work with its leadership in flux, during an especially critical time as competition in the AI chips market grows.

Industry observers note that on Tuesday’s third-quarter earnings call, an analyst from Bank of America Securities asked Kress directly about her “message” to Nvidia investors about talent retention, as well as the tech giant’s overall durability and financial strategy through this major upheaval. Kress replied that “probably the most important thing” company leaders are thinking through right now is stabilizing its employee ranks.

“We are always thinking about our employees. Like every community out there, there are diverse opinions,” Kress noted. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure they are safe and make sure the work can be done in the current environment.”.

In a brief question-and-answer session with Kress during the all-hands meeting Wednesday, Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky addressed how the company could maintain its prized culture going forward.

In a recent development, he recalled how he, Huang, and other cofounders thought it was “nonsense” to put cultural values up on posters. Instead, they want it instilled in “the way you behave, the way you work together and the way you work,” and he believes that will stand the test of time. “We’re going to be fine,” he said.

Kress ended the meeting, which lasted about 50 minutes, by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game.

In the third quarter, “every single person sings,” she remarked. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song… Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. Nvidia, we’ve got this.”.

Generative video is at a threshold moment: the models are now expressive enough to become the latest camera. The bottleneck is no longer the technical art of animation or the $100M budgets for film crews and visual effects; itâs human creativity and token inference. But video creators are not yet flying.

Itâs a gaping problem and is the biggest roadblock on the industryâs path to truly embracing AI.

Preview clears that block. An AI-native video creation and production platform built for professional creators, Preview combines a video timeline with an infinite canvas for ideation into one collaborative multiplayer workspace. Teams can generate with any model and track every character, location, and prop, with complete records of how every asset was made. It has been revealed that the MacBook Neo is on sale (finally), bringing the price down from $699 to $649. Fifty dollars might not sound like a lot, but it's the largest discount the MacBook Neo has ever received. The previous best deal was just $10 off. As Apple's first foray into the truly budget-tier laptop, the MacBook Neo's price has been stubbornly steady, more so than any other MacBook in the lineup.

The MacBook Neo does come with a number of compromises compared to the MacBook Air. The most notable is that it only has 8 GB of unified memory. This is what keeps it from feeling like a truly capable work or student laptop. If you spend most of your working hours sitting in front of a computer, the MacBook Air is worth springing for over the Neo.

Still, if you're after an affordable laptop that doesn't feel cheap, the MacBook Neo is excellent at playing that part. The display is bright and beautiful, and the build quality is as sturdy as you'd expect an Apple product to be. It even comes in a few unique colors. There are a lot of people who could just use a basic laptop, and $649 is a great price for one.

I should note that Apple does sell the laptop for $100 off as part of its education discount, but it requires having an active student ID. That's the way to go if you happen to be a student or teacher. For everyone else, though, this is the cheapest the MacBook Neo has been since late June, when Apple increased prices across the entire MacBook lineup.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM...
  • Recent findings suggest that the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM...
  • The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

Recent findings suggest that the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.

Recently, Alex Karp encouraged enterprises to âown the means of production.â Not long after, Satya Nadella declared that buying intelligence from a frontier lab is like paying twice: once with money, and once with the proprietary knowledge you reveal to make that intelligence useful.

The question everyone is asking: who should own the intelligence at the core of your business?

To be clear, owning your intelligence is not a mandate nor a recommendation to get off the labs. For many workloads, frontier APIs and agents are still the right answer. But across our portfolio, we are seeing more companies building their own AI capabilities for parts of their products, vertically integrating toward owning and shaping their weights.

In a recent development, A few weeks ago, Sequoia brought together a group of AI founders and builders for an event on owning your AI stack. We had Harvey give us the customer-back view. Then Mercor, Langchain, Trajectory, and Fireworks walked us through the technical building blocks in the post-training stack.

Across the talks, a clear playbook emerged.

Industry observers note that first, the open-weight frontier has moved faster than anticipated. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are extremely good! Training on open models used to be a treadmillâ¦ you mightâve spent months fine-tuning, and the next frontier release would erase your gains. Now, you can start from a baseline close to the frontier.

Industry observers note that second, the independent post-training stack has matured. Thanks to companies like Mercor and Fireworks, every manufacturer can access the technology stack of a frontier research lab, from training to inference to human or synthetic data. With strong evals, harness engineering, post-training, and online learning, open models can now beat frontier models in specific domains.

In a recent development, A year ago, you chose open weights when performance was something you could sacrifice. Now, it is becoming an existential and strategic question. The newest battleground is for the intelligence layer. Not your weights, not your product.

Recent findings suggest that thereâs no one-size-fits-all approach. In addition to performance, there may be slices of your product where renting intelligence becomes a constraint because ofâ¦.

Sources indicate that 1. Cost. The more successful your AI product, the higher your AI COGS. If inference costs scale directly with usage, owning the model is the best way to protect your margins.

Industry observers note that 2. Speed. If youâre operating in a domain like coding (tab autocomplete) or cybersecurity, a small distilled custom model might beat a large general one, because speed is so important.

Sources indicate that 3. Proprietary data. If your feedback, evals, customer interactions, or domain data are what make the system better, you might prefer that data stays within your walls.

Industry observers note that 4. Controlling your destiny. The app layer and the intelligence layer are starting to merge. The labs are moving up into product, and app companies are moving down into the training loops that define how the product thinks. Owning the product increasingly might mean controlling more of the learning loop and the intelligence itself (h/t Harvey Research, RampLabs, Glean, Factory, and more).

Recent findings suggest that assuming you've decided on your strategy for what to own vs. rent, the question becomes: how do you go from zero to one?

Build your team. Don't shoehorn this into a platform team. Owning your intelligence needs people playing offense: building evals, shaping data, experimenting with open models, tuning harnesses, and pushing performance in a domain. Small, de novo teams go very far here, partnering with half a dozen ecosystem partners. Harvey, for example, has done a surprising amount of research with a team of just seven people!

According to recent reports, make the work legible. Every buyer right now is choosing their AI champion. Increasingly, the tiebreaker is published research, benchmarks, or technical posts. If you choose to do wonderful research in-house, share it with the ecosystem.

Execute the technical steps. Weâve laid out a high level framework below.

Harveyâs Gabe Pereyra noted it well: "If you don't have a good benchmark, you can't train models.â.

In a recent development, an eval is a set of tasks that measures whether your system can do the work well. Every task contains a prompt, context the model can use, and a grader. Most evals start as a founder squinting at outputs and vibe-checking whether they feel right. The goal is to turn that judgement into something repeatable.

In a recent development, harvey built its Legal Agent Benchmark by turning real legal work into discrete tasks a model could be tested on. The first iteration includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.

According to recent reports, itâs important to have an eval before making the decision to own your intelligence. Once every forward pass has an eval, deciding which model to use can be a measured decision instead of a guess.

2/ Harness and context engineering.

An agent has three parts: the model, the context, and the harness. The harness governs the product logic around the model: routing, retrieval, tools, memory, fallbacks, and traces. Harrison Chaseâs simple framing was that "the main job of the harness is to bring context to the model at the right point in time." The more out of distribution the task is for the model, the worse the off-the-shelf harness will be.

A good harness lets you route tasks to the best model for your specific job, reuse the same evals across models, and decide what context and tools an agent gets. It also makes the agent inspectable. You can trace what context went in, which tools were called, and where it got stuck.

Recent findings suggest that post-training covers several techniques. The right one depends on what youâre trying to improve.

According to recent reports, lin Qiao laid it out: if the model is missing facts, you don't need to post-train - just use context or RAG. If the output format or behavior is wrong, use supervised fine-tuning. If the issue is product taste, use preference tuning. If the model needs to improve at a specialized task, use RL. If the model is too slow or expensive, distill it.

It has been revealed that the goal is to pick the lightest method that moves your eval. Then serve the model through the same harness and measure quality, latency, and cost as it runs.

Once the system has its pieces â evals, harness, and model â the final step is improving that system in production.

It has been revealed that arjun Karanam made a good point: models keep getting smarter, but every session feels like it's their first day on the job. You can put Terence Tao in an accounting firm, but chances are (at least on day 1) he wonât be the best accountant there. What's missing is experience, not intelligence. Agents create that experience as they run.

Sources indicate that A trajectory is the path through the task: the context the model saw, the tools and sub-agents it called, the answer it produced, and what the user edited, undid, or retried. Capturing those trajectories in a tool like LangChain's LangSmith is necessary to build a continuous production loop. A failed task becomes an eval. Missing information goes into context or memory. A bad tool response becomes a harness fix.

Buyer beware: owning your intelligence opens Pandoraâs box.

Industry observers note that the closed-model stack is simple. You call a frontier model, use an out-of-the-box harness (e.g., Claude Code or Codex), add prompts and context, and ship. That gives you a high floor, but also a lower ceiling.

Sources indicate that owning your stack means taking on more of the system yourself. The production stack becomes your open-source model, custom harness, tools, and context. The development stack becomes your proprietary evals, domain data, and online learning loop.

It is certainly more work! It potentially gives you a lower floor â but it also raises the ceiling.

In a recent development, the labs will keep building the giant brains. We should all use them.

But, in parallel, the best product companies are growing their own little geniuses: fast, opinionated, domain-obsessed, and tuned to the work they see. In a world where more companies take ownership of their own intelligence, the ecosystem flourishes and individuality triumphs.

Thatâs the promise of a world where companies own their intelligence. And weâre delighted to see the progress from the little guys, the startups that want to bring that world into existence.

The US Lost Its Measles Elimination Status. It’ll Take Years to Get It Back

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: two more people died from measles, bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and the country officially lost its status as a country that had eliminated the highly infectious disease.
  • The US eliminated measles in 2000 and maintained that status for 26 years.
  • Noel Brewer, a professor of health behavior at the University of North Carolina, presented a report last week to the Pan American Health Organization showing continuous measles transmission for at least 12 months in the US—erasing one of the nation’s greatest public health achievements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: two more people died from measles, bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and the country officially lost its status as a country that had eliminated the highly infectious disease.

The US eliminated measles in 2000 and maintained that status for 26 years. Now, the nation faces an uphill battle to vanquish the virus once more, and it will take years to be measles-free again.

Noel Brewer, a professor of health behavior at the University of North Carolina, presented a report last week to the Pan American Health Organization showing continuous measles transmission for at least 12 months in the US—erasing one of the nation’s greatest public health achievements.

Recent findings suggest that WIRED asked him how he felt after PAHO officials reached consensus the country was no longer measles-free. He paused.

“I have not actually thought about my reaction,” he notes. After a beat, he says that the loss is “a somber moment for public health” that’s particularly wrenching because it’s a “completely avoidable situation.” Mexico and Canada have managed to wind down their outbreaks, but “measles in America is a runaway train,” Brewer says. “There's no end in sight, and it may even be gaining speed.”.

PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr. officially confirmed the change in status on Tuesday. “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” he said at a press conference. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.” Bolivia and Mexico also lost their elimination status this year; Canada lost it a year ago.

Brewer presented three key lines of evidence showing that measles has become endemic in the US. The outbreak in Utah and Arizona has gone on for more than 12 months, and the US has had measles cases every week since January 20, 2025. The genomic data also demonstrates a great deal of similarity across states, indicating the clusters are closely linked—and each week, there are cases where the sources can’t be confirmed, indicating they didn’t come from travel or known contact with other patients.

“We have a problem on our hands,” states William Moss, epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins. And it’s not going away anytime soon. To reclaim its status as measles-free, the US will have to prove it has gone a full year without continued transmission. That’s unlikely to happen under the Trump administration—and its actions have made it more difficult for future leaders.

“Reestablishing elimination is not just about reporting fewer cases—it also requires convincing the world that we have a strong enough surveillance system to find cases and deaths,” Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University, tells WIRED in a text.

The fact that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments differ on how many people have died from measles “is a sign of dysfunction,” Nuzzo states. There have been 10 confirmed measles deaths so far this year—seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, and one in New York—but the CDC only lists six.

It has been revealed that such chaos also breeds distrust, states Frederic Bertley, president and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry. That's “a huge problem” for a public trying to parse who is telling the truth and whether they should listen, he says.

Even as measles was eliminated, anti-vaccine rhetoric began to rise, especially around the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Vaccination rates began falling—spurred in part by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an environmental lawyer turned anti-vaccine activist who published a now-retracted article alleging a link between vaccines and autism in 2005. He continued crusading against vaccines as head of Children’s Health Defense and at the helm of the Department of Health and Human Services during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration has done little to stop the outbreaks, cutting billions in funding from state, local, territorial, and tribal public health departments and offering conflicting messages on vaccines. During a televised February 2025 cabinet meeting following the first child death in a decade, Kennedy stated “it's not unusual, we have measles outbreaks every year.” The CDC hasn’t held a single press conference on measles throughout the entire outbreak; as PAHO was making its measles status announcement on Tuesday, HHS sent out an email about Kennedy’s cooking show.

According to recent reports, “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz remarked in a statement. “Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Kennedy posted on X that “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”.

In a recent development, to regain its elimination status, the US needs to address barriers to healthcare access, missed vaccination opportunities, misinformation, and vaccine hesitancy, Barbosa noted. That includes mounting wide-reaching vaccination campaigns, expanding laboratory testing capacity, and responding quickly to cases, including contact tracing. It’s the bread and butter of public health, but the longer it takes to create a comprehensive response, the more it will cost, experts warn.

Sources indicate that future efforts to contain measles will require “a stronger centralized federal response to these outbreaks” paired with support for “very local responses,” states Moss. That means identifying communities with longstanding under-vaccination and understanding why, he says, as well as improving trust in public health guidance.

“Immunity gaps” tend to concentrate in specific geographic areas and communities, and national or even state-level data can “mask these significant inequalities, providing an incomplete picture of the population's actual level of protection,” Barbosa remarked.

The CDC announced $100 million in August and September—more than a year after the outbreak began—to help fund state and regional efforts to combat measles, but Congress will need to allocate $100 million to $400 million more for measles elimination in coming months, Brewer claims.

Industry observers note that “More than 90 percent of children get the measles vaccine, Brewer points out. “This is a vaccine that has extraordinary public support, and it goes across the aisle.”.

Sources indicate that but to achieve herd immunity, vaccination rates need to be at least 95 percent due to how contagious the disease is. High transmissibility also means measles is very hard to uproot once it begins to spread.

Industry observers note that yet ending national measles transmission is “its own reward,” Brewer says. It spares children’s lives, keeps them out of hospitals, prevents blindness and other lifelong complications. “We no longer have that benefit,” he says. “Children are now being stalked by this incurable and deadly disease.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that two vulnerabilities in the India-based AI-driven debt collection platform CreditNirvana exposed 6.6 million accounts and about 315,000 call recordings from the company's agentic call center, according to research released on Wednesday.
  • According to recent reports, the bugs were patched in CreditNirvana's systems in June and were disclosed publicly in October.
  • “They fixed it in one day, which was great, but this is really a pretty significant case,” Zveare tells WIRED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that two vulnerabilities in the India-based AI-driven debt collection platform CreditNirvana exposed 6.6 million accounts and about 315,000 call recordings from the company's agentic call center, according to research released on Wednesday. Owned by the Indian fintech company Perfios, the platform is built to “read a borrower’s full context, decide the next best action, and execute it autonomously, continuously, and within policy.”.

According to recent reports, the bugs were patched in CreditNirvana's systems in June and were disclosed publicly in October. But independent researcher Eaton Zveare, who found and disclosed them, notes that, while the vulnerabilities were active, they exposed personal information on millions of borrowers. Details about financial collections are inherently—perhaps obviously—sensitive, because they relate to unpaid accounts or debts and often involve extensive documentation of people's personal histories.

“They fixed it in one day, which was great, but this is really a pretty significant case,” Zveare tells WIRED. “Some of the largest fintech firms across India use this company to autonomously collect debts, so they naturally hold data, including credit scores, call recordings, transcripts, court records, and other sensitive documents. There’s just so much in there that makes it a very sensitive issue.”.

CreditNirvana and Perfios did not return WIRED's requests for comment. Zveare states he worked directly with India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) to get the vulnerabilities fixed. CERT-In categorized one vulnerability as “high” severity and the other as “critical” severity.

The high-severity vulnerability impacted the call center data, exposing hundreds of thousands of calls as well as recommendations for next steps generated by the platform after calls were complete. It could also have been exploited to allow an attacker to manage AI agents within the platform and direct their own agentic campaigns.

According to recent reports, the critical severity vulnerability impacted CreditNirvana's main platform, and Zveare says it specifically exposed the data of three corporate customers—all prominent Indian financial services firms—using CreditNirvana for their collections. The data also exposed millions of individuals’ accounts, which contain credit reports, ID cards, case management details, and legal documents, along with certain types of communications, including millions of emails, texts, and call transcripts related to financial services, unpaid accounts, and collections. The vulnerability also could have been exploited by an attacker to track the location of human debt collection agents and for some administrative privileges within the system.

“Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to enumerate platform users, establish sessions as arbitrary users including administrative users, access and modify sensitive information with the privileges of the impersonated user,” CERT-In wrote.

Zveare says he is relieved that the issue was resolved promptly, but is conscious that the bugs were potentially present in CreditNirvana's systems for years. As AI is integrated into more and more automated systems, synthesizing data from a greater number of sources and using it to draw conclusions, Zveare says, the episode serves as “an crucial example of an AI-powered service having a very sensitive data exposure.”.

Announcing Sequoiaâs investment of $100M in Form Energy.

For me, it was always one of these companies that represented what venture capital was all about: a phenomenal team of entrepreneurs pursuing a world-changing idea that, if successful, could scale into a category-defining company.

Industry observers note that I first met Mateo Jaramillo, the CEO of Form Energy, in spring 2020. It was a memorable meeting because it was the first in-person founder meeting I had in the COVID pandemic and we were all wearing masks. At that time, Mateo described a simple idea: solar and wind were going to take over the grid, but we needed batteries to store that energy. Lithium-ion was a great chemistry for cars, and it could store grid-scale energy for 4-6 hours, but it was never going to store energy for multiple days. Thinking from first principles, Mateo, who previously started and ran Teslaâs energy business, had assembled the battery Avengers, including legendary battery scientist Yet-Ming Chiang as Chief Scientist and Billy Woodford as CTO. The team set their sights on building an iron-air battery: iron, because itâs cheap and abundant, and air, because itâs free. The goal was to turn those cheap materials into a battery that could compete with gas peaker plants on cost while delivering a clean and reliable baseload energy resource.

Industry observers note that knowing very little about batteries at the time, I reached out to a group of professors to diligence whether the science worked. I ended up selecting a Harvard professor and hired him as a consultant. At the end of the project, he gave us a thumbs up, and as a sign of his excitement, asked if he could roll his consulting fee into our investment.

When I arrived at Sequoia in mid-2023, Mateo was one of my first calls. At that time he was just starting construction on Form Energyâs first high-volume battery manufacturing facility, located on a shuttered steel mill site in West Virginia. I flew out for a factory visit with my partner Isaiah Boone in July 2024, and we were astounded. So many companies come to us talking about reindustrializing America, and here was a company that was actually doing it, and creating more than 400 upcoming jobs along the way. Given that China is the epicenter of battery manufacturing globally, we were energized by the potential to build a US national battery champion, starting with a fundamentally new technology, which is what America excels at.

In a recent development, the following year, the organization went through what is colloquially termed âproduction hell.â This is exactly what Tesla, SpaceX and others had gone through before them. If you really want to reindustrialize this country, these things donât happen overnight, and they are far from easy. Companies that go through this gauntlet come out sturdier and stronger. To Mateo and the teamâs credit, they doubled down. He had by then relocated his entire family from San Francisco to Western Pennsylvania, a short drive from the plant. Having experienced this type of scaling at Tesla, Mateo knew what to do: live it, sleep it, breathe it â until you've pulled through.

In a recent development, and pull through he did. I knew heâd turned the corner when finally, the firm received the order that everyone knew would eventually come: a large hyperscale project. Nine years in, Form had done the thing it set out to do: build battery systems that can compete with gas. In the meantime, luck worked in their favor too: AI provided a huge catalyst in the market, where suddenly rebuilding the grid went from ânice to haveâ to âneed to have.â As an AI investor, this company, which had spent years building deep relationships with utilities and regulators, was now in a prime position to serve emergent AI demand.

Isaiah and I flew back to West Virginia, exactly two years after our prior visit. This time we had an agenda: convince Mateo to partner with Sequoia. Although heâd already closed his Series G round, we persuaded him to let us invest. Initially, we proposed a $50M investment. But when Mateo came to present to the Sequoia partnership, they were so blown away by his clarity of vision and substantive, execution-oriented mindset that we upsized to $100M.

Sources indicate that as I wrote in my very first note to Sequoia in 2023 about Form Energy, this is a company like SpaceX or Nvidia where it can take a decade to get off the ground, but once you get off the ground, the market opportunity is very large â Form is addressing a terawatt-scale market. The opportunity to now scale up from a handful of initial projects toward completely transforming the US grid is tremendous. Not only that, but it is no longer optional â it is something that we as a country will absolutely have to do for AI to achieve its long-term potential.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Change has always been the fundamental operational signal in infrastructure. Empirik is turning that signal into the foundation for autonomous, agentic infrastructure engineering.

Change has always been the fundamental operational signal in infrastructure. Empirik is turning that signal into the foundation for autonomous, agentic infrastructure engineering.

Industry observers note that this one started close to home. Before Sequoia, our Chief Digital and Information Officer, Avon Puri, had spent two decades running IT and infrastructure at scale as SVP & CIO at Rubrik, and VP of Engineering and Applications at VMware (also my alma mater in the tech world). Avon and Sudheer Dhurjati, who worked alongside him at all three companies, watched the same story repeat: enterprise infrastructure operates in a reactive posture. Companies spend tens of billions of dollars on observabilityâmetrics, logs, and tracesâto tell us when a system is failing. But traditional observability is inherently post-mortem.

In a recent development, the real driver of infrastructure behavior is change: a new identity policy is attached, a new Terraform provider completes, or a feature flag flips in production. However, change has been treated as an administrative process constraint, a static ticket, an approval form, or as tribal knowledge buried in email or Slack. It was sometimes recorded for compliance, but never truly put to work to do actual infrastructure engineering jobs.

If you understand the real-time stream of changes across every layer of the environment, you don't just get better alertsâyou unlock true autonomy. Every change reflects an engineer's intent; once a system can interpret that intent and assess its impact, it can decide whether to act on its own or loop in a human. By bringing agentic capabilities to infrastructure, you solve the full lifecycle of infrastructure engineering jobs, shifting from a reactive firefighting posture to a proactive one.

According to recent reports, that insight became the founding pillar behind Empirik. Avon and Sudheer built the initial version inside Sequoia. We saw companies rushing to deploy AI agents to automate coding, marketing, and many other enterprise processes, but infrastructure was the one place nobody was modernizing. After the same rigorous evaluation any other Sequoia investment goes through, Empirik spun out as an independent firm. And now, itâs under the leadership of CEO Kartik Chandrayana, a repeat founder who sold his first company, Twin Prime, to Salesforce, then spent five years as Salesforce's VP of Product for Observability and Significant Data, and most recently was CPO at Quantum Metric. Today, we're excited to share that Empirik is emerging from stealth with $21M in funding.

According to recent reports, agentic coding has taken off because code lives in version-controlled repositories that make a system's architecture and intent legible to a model. Infrastructure has never had that foundation. Infrastructure-as-code is a good start, but because it represents a declared state and not what's actually running in production, it's inherently behind. There's no unified, real-time representation of an organization's infrastructure across the maze of cloud resources, Kubernetes, networking, identity, and legacy systems. Infrastructure does not have the notion of a pull request; instead, every change still runs through tribal knowledge and institutional memory of people rather than the machine rigor of software.

It has been revealed that observability is already a large, proven marketâDatadog, Dynatrace, and Splunk are behemoths with billions in revenue. But all of observability is built to measure symptoms: latency spiked, errors climbed, a pod crashed. Empirik's bet is that there's a fourth pillar hiding in plain sightâthe changes themselves. Instead of "latency in service X increased 300% in the last 24 hours," Empirik tells you, "Joe deployed a Terraform provider that shut down three VMs in AWS"âthe actual cause and context, not just the symptom. And why stop there? With Empirik, you can actually warn or stop Joe even before he deploys Terraform because Empirik computes that risk at the inception of change.

It has been revealed that as Kartik describes it: infrastructure today is where software engineering was three years agoâbefore Claude Code and Cursor, when every action needed a human in the loop because there was no reliable map of the system to reason over. Empirik is building that map, and putting it to work as the Autonomous Infra EngineerâAI that can safely strategy, reason about, and operate enterprise infrastructure. It's already plugged into agentic workflows via MCP, connecting directly into tools like Claude and ChatGPT, so that humans and agents alike can reason over infrastructure change with real contextânot guesswork.

Under the hood is an infrastructure compiler. Just as a traditional compiler translates source code into executable software, Empirik converts metadata from a customerâs clouds, identity providers, CI/CD, and SaaS systems into a live, unified operational graphâmapping thousands of relationships between assets and accounts. That graph is how the product knows, in real time, what changed, who changed it, and whether itâs the reason something broke.

Recent findings suggest that what I particularly appreciate about the teamâs approach is that they didnât take shortcuts. Itâs easy for modern startups to build exclusively for greenfield Kubernetes or a single public cloud provider. But from day one, Avon, Sudheer, and Kartik designed Empirik for the reality of the Fortune 500 enterprise: a complex, multi-decade hybrid stack spanning public clouds, legacy on-prem infrastructure, identity layers, and critical SaaS apps. An infrastructure graph that only sees half your environment misses the mark for an enterprise buyer. Empirikâs graph connects the entire surface area so teams and agents have complete operational context.

The traction backs up the thesis. Fortune500 Financial enterpriseâs interest in the product traces directly back to a P0 outage caused by an unapproved change. TCBPay, a payment processing manufacturer with $1.5B+ in annual volume now catches sensitive config file changes in 10 seconds, down from 30 minutes. Avahi, an MSP, integrated Empirik within their GitHub Actions to evaluate and block risky changes at the source. Guardant Health found Empirik so valuable that it expanded its deployment from production to all dev environments, and even expanded to on-prem. And a global Fortune-50 CPG company is also expanding its footprint, relying on Empirik to drive most of its agentic and autonomous infra roadmap. Empirik is now processing millions of raw change and telemetry events every week, over dependency graphs spanning a few million resources across all major clouds and on-prem systems. Customers are reporting benefits in multiple domains: preventing risky changes from making it to production, detecting unapproved changes, faster incident response, making rollback decisions, and detecting drifts, among others.

The success is no surprise given this team. Avon and Sudheer are two of the best operators we know, and they built Empirik the way they'd have wanted it built for themselves. Kartik, meanwhile, has firsthand expertise in shipping observability products at enterprise scale. Most enterprises still can't answer that simple but critical question: what changed, and did that cause the incident? Empirik is building the system of record for that questionâfor humans today, and for the agents that will increasingly be making those changes themselves tomorrow.

The ‘GTA 6’ Work Blackout Is Here

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, somewhere out there, right at this moment, a couple is probably still negotiating the final terms of a contract that permits one partner to play Grand Theft Auto VI around the clock for an entire week following its Thursday release.
  • So don’t be surprised if a console owner in your life is curiously unavailable between now and Thanksgiving.
  • Especially within the tech and gaming industries, the expectation is that many developers won’t be clocking in on Thursday or Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, somewhere out there, right at this moment, a couple is probably still negotiating the final terms of a contract that permits one partner to play Grand Theft Auto VI around the clock for an entire week following its Thursday release. Adults who grew up on the felony-based video game franchise are taking steps to secure sick days—and some, no doubt, are granting their own kids permission to stay home from school (despite warnings from their teachers). Streamers on Twitch and YouTube stand ready to conquer the enhanced and expanded virtual domain of Vice City, seeking out every last Easter egg.

So don’t be surprised if a console owner in your life is curiously unavailable between now and Thanksgiving. The 13-year-wait for this latest installment of the series has felt interminable enough to inspire a meme used in reaction to any surprising or unprecedented news: “We got [fill in the blank] before GTA VI.”.

Especially within the tech and gaming industries, the expectation is that many developers won’t be clocking in on Thursday or Friday. (GTA VI officially launches for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S at midnight local time on Thursday, November 19, according to publisher Rockstar Games.).

“I’m not going to question whether folks are really sick on their sick days or how they spend a vacation day,” says Mike, an executive of a gaming studio with more than a thousand employees, who requested a pseudonym to avoid damaging professional relationships within the industry. “I want them to spend time engaging with the medium we love, and there’s no question that playing lots of video games helps you make video games.”.

Recent findings suggest that in October, the HR software organization BambooHR concluded through data analysis and a survey of salaried workers that the PTO request rate for November 19 is nearly 13 percent higher than equivalent days in past years, while Xbox is running a promotional campaign in which gamers can generate notes from a Dr. Xbox (DJ Khaled in glasses and a lab coat) claiming that they have a “Vitamin G” deficiency and are unable to work.

A few companies are getting ahead of the productivity slump; the hardware and software manufacturer Logitech, for example, unveiled earlier this month that all 7,000 employees would be granted a paid day off for gaming, to be scheduled any time within a year or so. In announcing the policy, the manufacturer cited internal studies on the ways that gaming may potentially improve job performance and mental health.

Sources indicate that riot Games, the publisher behind League of Legends and Valorant, has likewise made arrangements for the blockbuster event. “We have an open PTO policy, and we’ve seen leaders encourage their teams to enjoy the first day of release,” Joe Hixson, Riot Games vice president of communications, tells WIRED. “On our main campus, we'll be celebrating with a special-themed lunch menu and snacks that pay homage to the game. We also expect to see people firing it up in our console rooms during breaks and after hours.”.

Riot additionally offers the Play Fund, a stipend of $25 a month for employees to spend on gaming titles across platforms and genres. “It makes us better developers by deepening our understanding of what makes a great player experience,” Hixson notes.

Recent findings suggest that mike tells WIRED that on in-office workdays, the tech giant has a typical absentee rate of 5 to 7 percent due to vacations, illness, travel, and the like. He estimates that on Thursday, it will be more like 10 or 12 percent. “Now, on the Friday, will there be some number of employees who are ‘working’ when they’re at home but also suspiciously slow to answer messages while they have major chunks of their calendar blocked out for ‘deep individual work?’” indicates the studio leader. “Yeah, probably.”.

But it’s hardly unusual in the business for people to select their days off to accommodate a major game release, Mike says. In 2023, he was out for three days to play The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, which he recalls as “paradise.”.

It has been revealed that that mentioned, he notes that the next leap forward for GTA is no ordinary affair. The hype for this franchise, he explains, “breaks containment,” reaching people who have not bought a fresh title in years.

According to recent reports, that’s why even companies without ties to gaming culture have been making allowances for so-called Grand Theft Auto Flu. On Monday, the social team for the luxury real estate firm Serhant posted a video of CEO Ryan Serhant (also the host of the Netflix reality show Owning Manhattan) agreeing with an employee that if the clip garnered 400,000 likes, the office would close for GTA day. “You’ll never get that,” Serhant predicted.

According to recent reports, the post picked up 1.4 million likes within 24 hours, prompting an update on Tuesday: The firm would honor Serhant’s promise. “We are significant supporters of our team, their passions both in and out of real estate, and all things culture and tech,” Serhant noted in a statement to WIRED, noting that “13 years of anticipation deserves a day off.” The tech giant announced a floating holiday to staff on Wednesday, to be used any time before the end of 2026.

Also on Wednesday, Arizona Beverages revealed a sweepstakes for social media followers who may have felt they couldn’t afford to miss a work shift. Dropping a PTO request for GTA day in the comment section, the company said, would enter that person for a chance to win $500 to cover their lost hours.

Recent findings suggest that with this level of fanfare, nearly 16 million preorders bringing in revenue of $1.5 billion, and expectations of 45 million sales in its launch quarter, GTA VI is poised to be the most significant entertainment event of the year and the biggest video game of all time. It’s little wonder, then, that some have warned about the global economy slowing down this week as fans ignore their email inboxes and Slack messages to indulge in some extended role-play as streetwise criminals. One economist has estimated that the GTA release could cost the US economy $1 billion in lost productivity.

Mike isn’t buying this, however, arguing that the hype about “how GTA will impact the GDP or cause a failure of the power grid or whatever are just silly.” He points out that “PC is the biggest individual platform, and the PC launch timing is still unclear.” Neither have Rockstar and Take-Two unveiled a launch date for the game’s online multiplayer mode; only the single-player experience will be available on Thursday.

Andy Garin, an associate professor of economics at Carnegie Mellon University, also finds the concerns about sluggish market activity to be overblown.

Recent findings suggest that “Speculation about a hit to productivity around these kinds of events pops up a lot, particularly during the Olympics or World Cup, when time zone differences mean major events are during the workday,” Garin says. “I don't think the release date of GTA VI will be that different than these sort of events that happen all the time, particularly if workers are using their allotted PTO or scheduling flexibility baked into their jobs.”.

Industry observers note that malcolm Robinson, who has a YouTube channel dedicated to gaming and works at a veterans hospital, tells WIRED that the GTA release just happens to fall on his day off. “I strategy on playing it for about eight to 12 hours straight on the first night,” he says.

Others have had no difficulty setting that time aside. One redditor who works as the distribution coordinator for a chain of auto shops in Colorado and requested anonymity out of concern for professional consequences states that he would have called in sick on Thursday but had the option to use PTO. His supervisor asked if it was to play GTA, which he confirmed. “He was like, ‘I get it, enjoy,’” this gamer reports. He intends to play along with his girlfriend, who is also taking the day off, and is excited to “sink my teeth into it before the entire thing gets spoiled.”.

James Lord, a data entry coordinator in Edmonton, Alberta, tells WIRED that he initially offered to let his team take Thursday off for GTA purposes. When none of them expressed interest in the game, he says, he “jumped at the opportunity” to claim the day for himself. He’s been playing Grand Theft Auto since the original top-down POV game for the PC came out in the late 1990s.

Lord, too, is wary of spoilers—he locked down his social media on Tuesday night to avoid any—but nostalgia and lifelong relationships are even better reasons to jump into GTA VI as soon as he can. He’s going to boot up the game while on a call with his brother, who lives across the country, and they’ll be joined by friends living in Pennsylvania and Texas. It’s a reunion experience that wouldn’t be possible without a break from the 9-to-5 job.

“We lead busy lives now,” Lord reflects, “so having to set time aside for the game of the decade is important to us.”.

But as we ran our references on them across the Israeli cybersecurity ecosystem, the same answer kept coming back: they would be among the strongest founding teams in the country. One of the former commanders of Unit 8200 told us Yair was "the only person I have ever thought had everything required to one day command Unit 8200" â about as strong an endorsement as exists in Israeli tech. Niv is a technical outlier who led 8200âs most important vulnerability research department, building a network of elite technical talent. Yair finished his service on a Thursday, and we shook hands on a seed investment that Saturday, which tells you all you need to know about the pace at which this team operates.

Sources indicate that well before Yair and Niv started building a defensive security product, they built MOAK, the "Mother of All KEVs," an agentic workflow that produces working exploits for freshly published vulnerabilities with no human in the loop. In one demonstration, MOAK exploited a React vulnerability in 21 minutes, versus the six days or so it takes a typical enterprise to roll out a patch. They released it publicly, to ring an alarm bell that the industry was badly underestimating the leverage attackers can now get from AI, and that defensive tooling needed to catch up.

Industry observers note that the day developers started importing other people's packages instead of writing everything themselves, software acquired a supply chain. It then took two decades and a number of painful incidents, from log4j to Solarwinds, to build the machinery for inspecting what was coming in. Agents now have precisely the same problem, except that their supply chain is assembled at runtime and often nobody is inspecting it at all. An enterprise agent consumes skills, plugins, MCP servers, sub-agents, hooks, commands and rules â each running with the agentâs own permissions, inside a userâs environment, against a userâs data. Usually, theyâre installed with the care most of us would give a browser extension.

Air has spent the past several months demonstrating the stakes. They wrote a deliberately malicious skill and watched multiple AI marketplaces wave it through as safe. Their Story of Skills research demonstrated a researcher-built malicious skill reaching more than 26,000 agents through a trusted marketplace and social media, with every scanner clearing it. Then they published SkillJacking, which showed 925 live skills were pulling their dependencies and prompts from dead links; Air registered those links and took control of the roughly 134,000 agents that had installed them. Every public scanner they tested missed the problems completely.

Sources indicate that the same day, Yair and Niv shipped ScanAir, an OWASP-aligned scanner for agentic skills. That sequence â find the hole, prove it, publish it, then ship the thing that closes it â is the pattern we like most about this team.

According to recent reports, today, Air has three products that between them cover the full lifecycle of an agent's add-ons. Air Filter vets every add-on before an agent is permitted to consume it, using static analysis, dependency checks and sandbox detonation. It then intercepts unsafe installations in real time and offers safe alternatives in their place. Air Defend monitors what agents actually do once theyâre running and provides security operations teams with detection and response capabilities for agent behavior. Finally, Air Control handles posture and policy, from knowing which agents exist and what theyâre allowed to touch, to revoking a bad skill across thousands of agents at once. Think of it like home security: Air Filter is the locks and the childproofing, Air Defend is the cameras and the person watching them, and Air Control is the panel by the door â every entry point accounted for, every code assigned, and all of them revocable at once.

Every couple of years, the best cyber talent coming out of Unit 8200 consolidates around a handful of teams. First it was Wiz, Cyera, and, Island; then it was Eon, Glow, Decart, and Kela; now it is Air. Yair and Niv are smart, hungry natural leaders who have proven their ability to attract extreme talent density; in only a few short months they have built a cracked team of the very best. We at Sequoia are proud to led their seed round, and to now double down in their Series A.

According to recent reports, as enterprises move toward handing agents real authority over real systems, every CISO will be asked the same questions: what is our agent actually running, where did it come from, and who checked it? Today, few have complete answers. But Air is building the system of record that will.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a six-year-old elephant seal in Tasmania named Neil who has a taste for light property damage during the winter months. Now, the state has a management plan.

Neil's annual “hauling out” and subsequent misadventures on the southeastern part of the island has delighted locals, making him a local mascot and a viral social media star.

It has been revealed that but Neil’s on-land hijinks—as he experiences his yearly “catastrophic molt,” during which he, like all elephant seals, sheds and replaces his top level of fur and epidermis— has also created headaches for local officials. Neil, who weighs over 2,000 pounds, has destroyed walkways, flattened bollards, bowled through fences, and rammed vehicles. The enormous and growing public interest in Neil has also been a source of concern, as officials spend tens of thousands of Australian dollars to keep the public at a safe distance from him.

The Tasmanian government, finding itself in a precarious position, has finally decided to take action. The Department of Natural Resources and Environment published a 27-page dossier this week titled “Neil the Seal Management Proposal.”.

“The purpose of this Plan is to set out a framework for managing the resident elephant seal known as Neil in Tasmania, recognising the complex challenges associated with his recurring haul out period,” the dossier states.

Neil has a dedicated task force to monitor his whereabouts and according to the dossier, they would take a “non-intervention,” hands-off approach if he hauls out in a secluded location. They’d keep tabs on Neil from a distance, erecting signs around the area to alert the public of Neil’s presence while advising them to keep their distance. Should the public tempt fate and approach Neil, the task force can call in security personnel to keep people and the seal safe.

Sources indicate that the second contingency proposal is titled “on-site seal management,” which would be necessary if Neil comes ashore in a more public location, and has immediate access to roads and critical infrastructure that up the odds of molting-induced mayhem. One proposed management option involves “hazing,” which would essentially treat Neil like a frat pledge. The dossier doesn’t get into specifics—ostensibly there’s no paddling or eating a live goldfish involved—but highlights what it calls a “non-violent method of using deterrents and negative associations to disturb an animal, compelling them to move,” which can include “controlled visual, tactile and vocal stimuli where appropriate.”.

The document also notes that Neil appears to be adapting to and thus eluding “standard management practices,” meaning that the task force needs to stay nimble in coming up with fresh methods to curb Neil’s taste for antics.

Tasmanian officials also propose “seal enrichment,” which they say would be used in tandem with other management options, to redirect “natural exploratory behaviors” (like engaging with infrastructure) towards decoy items “designed to withstand repeated interaction.”.

In a recent development, officials also say that despite their best efforts to avoid Neil-related interruptions to daily life, “significant events,” such as road closures, public safety incidents, relocation or translocation activities, or wildlife-born diseases, are still liable to happen. During such events, members of the public are advised to contact the Marine Mammal Hotline, also known as “0427 WHALES.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
