📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we externalized our muscles and built the modern world. Now we are externalizing our minds.

Sources indicate that we externalized our muscles and built the modern world. Now we are externalizing our minds.

Most mornings I ride to work in a Waymo.

Sources indicate that the car is doing physical work: five thousand pounds of metal and glass moving across the San Francisco Bay Area. The car is also doing cognitive work: reading the road and making predictions that result in 17x fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers.

The experience asks nothing of my muscles and nothing of my mind. Both have been externalized.

This one ride encapsulates two revolutions. The physical one is 200 years old. The cognitive one has barely started.

It seems the mood around that second revolution is a cocktail of optimism, skepticism and anxiety. Talk of a singularity. Recursive self-improvement. Trillion-dollar clusters. Superintelligence. Unemployment. Social disruption. A race between superpowers. Itâs dizzying.

My view is far from dizzying. I think we have already undergone a transition that rhymes with the AI revolution in the coming decades: the Industrial Revolution.

We can bifurcate work into physical work and cognitive work. Most valuable tasks necessitate both.

In a recent development, agriculture is one of the oldest examples. Working the land took muscle, ours and our animals', for ten thousand years. It also took insight: reading the seasons, observing which seed produced which yield, etc.

It has been revealed that the two kinds of work are different. Physical work is force times distance: moving mass through space. Cognitive work is thinking. But both are scarce, have a price, and get applied to a task somebody wants done. In both cases when price collapses, supply floods in. In most cases, demand expands to meet supply.

For most of history, nearly all physical work done for humans was done by muscle, ours and animals. The chart above goes flat before the 1700s, and the flat part runs back as far as we do.

In the late 1700s and early 1800s things started to change. First steam, then combustion and the electric motor. Each wave took a larger share of the world's physical work. Over the course of about two centuries, physical work went from 99% biological to 99.9% machine.

Today the results are everywhere. The screen youâre reading this on. Nearly every article of clothing youâre wearing. The plane that carried you on your last trip. The lattice of ships, trains and trucks behind every ordinary product in modern life. Human muscle is a rounding error in the global energy budget.

For most of history, essentially all cognitive work was done by humans (plus a small assist from animals like the sheepdog). On top of that sat a thin mechanical sliver: tools that computed a little, like the clock or Pascal's mechanical calculator.

It has been revealed that then came electronic computation. Inside a century, it spread from simple calculations and spreadsheets to trillions then quadrillions of operations running 24 hours per day. Navigating your commute, processing payroll, pricing your insuranceâ¦this is all cognitive work done by machines.

The next wave is neural networks. This wave drastically expands the types of cognitive work machines can do. Just as combustion engines magnified the scope of the Industrial Revolution, neural networks are set to accelerate the Cognitive Revolution.

Sources indicate that A century ago, 99% of cognitive work was done by humans. In the near future, 99.9% will be done by machines. Not because humans will think less, but because machines will compute much much more.

In a recent development, the parallel in the two curves is stark. The Cognitive Revolution will look a lot like the Industrial Revolution. But it will be bigger and much faster. Divide the global economy by the nature of work, and cognitive and physical work could split a ~$120 trillion world economy roughly equally. The physical half has been mechanizing for 200 years. The cognitive half has barely started.

According to recent reports, so what actually happens in a revolution like this? Letâs run it back.

Sources indicate that the industrial age required massively scaling up input commodities: first coal and iron, then oil and steel. Iron was made by a process known as puddling. Steel was made by a process called the Bessemer process.

Industry observers note that the parallel is clear: electricity and compute. The âprocessâ here are algorithms like the Transformer.

Recent findings suggest that the providers of those components were the titans of their era. Carnegie and U.S. Steel, Rockefeller and Standard Oil. Process designers like Henry Bessemer. The modern equivalents are Jensen Huang's NVIDIA, Morris Changâs TSMC, authors of the Transformer paper, founders of the great Model Labs and the hyperscalers pouring trillions into data centers. Nations that once measured power in refining capacity will measure it in grid capacity and intelligence output.

Industry observers note that A unit of mechanical work in 1900 cost a small fraction of what it cost in 1800. That collapse in price made mass production possible, and made the revolution universal rather than a curiosity for the rich.

In a recent development, the cost of cognition is collapsing faster. Intelligence per Watt has been falling more than 10x per year.

With price decline, customers will buy wildly, absurdly more intelligence.

Nobody in 1800 flew to Tokyo, shipped strawberries across a hemisphere in January, or air-conditioned Phoenix. All these are physical processes that either were impossible or impractically expensive.

Demand for physical work exploded once new technologies were invented and price collapsed. William Jevons identified the phenomenon in 1865: more efficient engines did not reduce Britain's coal consumption. They multiplied it.

Cognition will follow the same pattern, and here the latent demand is almost unbounded in scale. Most problems on Earth at the moment go un-thought-about, because thinking is expensive. A doctor has limited time and doesnât review the latest literature. A radiologist studies a scan for minutes instead of hours. A small business owner has no budget for a financial analyst.

When cognition costs approach zero, every curiosity can get a research team.

Sources indicate that the amount of thinking done by machines will grow by orders of magnitude. Which raises the question, what will all that thinking be spent on?

The primal application of the Industrial Revolution was spinning textiles.

Spinning and weaving were skilled work. Textile makers were respected in your society: years of apprenticeship, a craft guild, a trade the family had held for generations. In 1764, James Hargreaves built the Spinning Jenny, which let one person spin eight threads at once, and later eighty. Clothing prices fell rapidly and global clothing consumption exploded.

The big change was the human moving from performing the task to supervising it. One person tending a frame produced what a room of hand-spinners once had.

The primal skilled application of this era is AI coding. Writing software is our era's elite craft: highly skilled, highly paid, a decade to master. And it is the first cognitive task where the pattern has fully flipped. The machine now completes most of the work, and the engineer's job is to direct, review and correct it. Itâs no accident that this is where the Cognitive Revolution found its first commercial traction.

While textiles kicked off the industrial revolution, they did not define it. The ultimate innovation of the industrial revolution was the automobile: a civilization grew around it, including suburbs, highways, supply chains, and the entire geography of modern life.

Industry observers note that coding agents are our Spinning Jennies: the first act, automating a skilled cognitive task. The automobile of this revolution has probably not been built yet. It will be something that was impossible while thinking was scarce.

My candidates: science conducted at machine speed, the personal agent that serves your life the way a chief of staff organizes a CEO's, or something in how humans connect and coordinate. In 1800, the automobile would have been hard to predict.

In 1800, over 75% of American workers worked the land. Machines came for that work. Today, farming is about 1% of U.S. employment. By the pessimists' arithmetic, over 74% of the country should be unemployed.

Instead we invented work no farmer in 1800 could have named. Radiologist. Software engineer. Podcast producer. Flight attendant. The machines did not end labor. They eliminated categories of work and expanded the total amount of it. There are more people employed today than at any point in human history, and they are vastly richer than their ancestors. All of my ancestors worked in agriculture 100 years ago. I knew all four of my grandparents, all of whom were born to farming families. None of them finished their lives in agriculture. All of them considered the non-agricultural work they did at the end of their lives more pleasant and prosperous than the hard agricultural work their families had done for generations.

According to recent reports, the same is taking shape in the Cognitive revolution. Despite the âspinning Jennyâ phenomena in AI coding, data supports that demand for software engineers, the most AI exposed occupation was accelerating higher, has inflected. In the coming week, we proposal to share data supporting inflections in hiring in other areas being transformed by AI, including Legal Services and Financial Services.

It has been revealed that machines doing cognitive work will not mean humans stop doing cognitive work any more than the tractor meant humans stopped doing physical things. The specific tasks change. The junior analyst who builds the model by hand becomes the person directing a hundred models. Further, categories of work we cannot at the moment name will grow the way "engineer" became a job following the invention of the engine during the Industrial Revolution.

Like in the industrial revolution, the aggregate story will be triumphant. But, the individual story will frequently not be. The handloom weavers of Lancashire were not retrained into locomotive engineers. Many of them simply lost, and their losses spanned a generation. The economic historian Robert Allen gave the period a name: Engels' pause. Between 1780 and 1840, British output per worker rose 46%. Real wages rose 12%.

Luddites were not wrong about their own lives, but about their childrenâs and grandchildren's. Between 1840 and 1900, British output per worker rose 90% and real wages rose 123%. Wages caught up to productivity, and then outran it.

A pause is not a foregone conclusion. Mark Zuckerberg put this well recently: âThere is no rule that AI must increase automation faster than it increases individuals' capabilities or demand for latest skills.â Humanityâs demand for new skills, for better and worse, will be insatiable.The difference this time is speed. The Industrial Revolution gave a farmhand's son forty years to become a factory hand. This revolution may offer five. Society's shock absorbers, like education, retraining, and safety nets, were designed for the old clock. The central policy question of the next two decades is whether we can help humans transform as fast as the jobs do.

The Industrial Revolution created the modern education system, in at least two ways.

Recent findings suggest that first, it made mass education possible. When most of humanity had to work the fields, children were labor. Machines taking over the physical work is what freed children to sit in classrooms and freed societies to fund them. The modern university exists because society no longer needed every able body in the field, and could redirect a civilization's youth toward cognitive skill-building instead.

Second, and less flatteringly, it shaped what education became. The factory needed workers who could read instructions, do arithmetic, show up on time and perform standardized tasks in synchronized shifts. So we built schools that look suspiciously like factories: Bells. Rows. Fixed schedules. Batch processing by age. Standardized outputs. Mass education was, in large part, industrial job training.

The Cognitive Revolution upends both of these dynamics. If machines do the cognition, the factory-model school is the equivalent of training for hand-spinning. But the deeper change is on the delivery side. For all of history, the binding constraint on education was the ratio of teachers to students. Benjamin Bloom quantified the cost of that constraint in 1984: the average student tutored one-to-one with mastery learning outperformed 98% of students in a conventional classroom.

That constraint is dissolving. The marginal cost of an infinitely patient, endlessly knowledgeable tutor is approaching zero. Hybrid human-AI tutors are found to be more effective and less costly than traditional education. Further, fresh hybrid AI approaches could help spread education in parts of the world where public education has been prohibitively expensive.

Modern medicine was also built by the industrial revolution. Mass production gave us penicillin at scale, refrigeration that made vaccines deliverable, and the chemical industry that spawned the pharmaceutical industry.

Recent findings suggest that the Cognitive Revolution pushes this much further. Drug discovery is a search across a space too large for humans to comprehend, which is exactly the work that scales best when cognition gets cheap. By predicting structures for virtually every known protein, AlphaFold solved a challenge where even minor breakthroughs previously demanded entire lifelong careers.Thousands of diseases right now have no treatment, not because they are unsolvable but because the cost of investigating each was never justified by the number of patients. When that cost collapses, the long tail becomes addressable the way every other latent demand does.

Curing disease has been the ambition of every generation of physicians. This is the first generation where the binding constraint is no longer how many of them there are.

Industry observers note that then there are the doctors in clinical practice. We face a massive shortage of physicians both in the United States and globally, with demand far exceeding supply. This issue is deeply personal to me, as I have long seen healthcare workers in my family stretched thin attempting to meet patient needs. Cheaper, accessible cognitive tools will not lead to doctors taking time off; instead, they will allow more patients to receive higher-quality care. Given the virtually limitless demand for better healthcare, scalable intelligence can help shift our medical model from reactive treatment to proactive care.The Shape of Daily Life.

Sources indicate that beyond work and school, the Industrial Revolution changed the texture of ordinary life so thoroughly that we now mistake its artifacts for human nature. The Cognitive Revolution will change them once again.

Recent findings suggest that clock time. Before factories, rural work followed seasons and sunlight. But a factory owner needed hundreds of people to start and stop simultaneously. The machine ran on a schedule, so the humans had to. Rigid shifts, the workday, the work week, modern timekeeping itself: these are industrial inventions, barely two centuries old. The Cognitive Revolution loosens their grip. When your machine colleagues work continuously and asynchronously, there is no reason for a hundred humans to think in unison from nine to five. Work drifts back toward task rhythms rather than clock rhythms.

Home and Work. Work happened in and around the home for most of human history: the farm, the cottage workshop, the family trade. Industrialization pulled the workplace out of domestic space because the work had to happen where the machine was. The daily commute is the residue of that separation. The Cognitive Revolution reverses it, because the machine now lives everywhere and one of the most powerful tools in history fits in your pocket. Home and work are recombining.

Global trade and power. Industrial nations imported raw materials and exported finished goods, an asymmetry that drove imperialism. The new raw materials are energy, compute and algorithms. The finished good is intelligence. The last time this asymmetry appeared, it defined a century of international order and disorder: the same industrial base that laid rail and poured steel also eventually created atomic bombs. Intelligence will be dual-use in the same way, and faster. The Industrial Revolution lifted humanity, but its safeguards arrived late. This time we should try to be earlier.

Follow the thread and you eventually arrive at the real question underneath the anxiety about AI: If the machines do the thinking, what are we for?

The last revolution already answered the physical version. At the end of the Industrial Revolution, humans did not stop moving their bodies. We remained embodied creatures.

In a recent development, proportionally, fewer of us work intense physical jobs. However, far more of us move for sport and purpose: we run marathons, climb mountains, and pay for the privilege of holding yoga poses in uncomfortably hot rooms. Along the way, we created sports-leagues and even the modern Olympics were the result of the Industrial Revolution.

Recent findings suggest that cognition will make the same migration. Chess is a clean example. Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997 and Kasparov later half-jokingly described himself as the first knowledge worker whose job was threatened by a machine. Chess did not die. More people play it today than at any point in history. When AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, researchers found that the novelty of moves played by human Go professionals increased significantly afterward. Superhuman machines made human play more creative, not less. The âcentaurâ era of machine-human collaboration was brief, but the human era never ended.

It has been revealed that critics of this essay will argue that âthis time is different.â Specifically, they will point out that humans were the smartest animals on earth and that this is the first time something uniquely human is displaced by a machine. That is incorrect. It is incorrect for at least two reasons. First, thinking is not uniquely human. Animals think. Even nature follows complex and âintelligentâ patterns. Second, there are many uniquely human skills that machines exceed already. For example, making fire is strictly a human skillâ¦and now your stove does it with the press of a button. Same with writing and transferring information (the internet). Same with making tools (us and chimpanzees), but now machines make most of our tools. And then Einstein reinvented it completely-- humans making a comeback -- with a new human thought experiment that was needed to accurately plot the orbit of Mercury! Flight was a super-human task until airplanes made it accessible. This time is different, but not that different.What stays economically human the longest is what was never really cognition to begin with: wanting things, choosing between them, being accountable for the choice, and being trusted by other people. The machine can draft the treaty. Someone still has to sign it. Over 2500 years ago, Greek philosopher Protagaros wrote "Man is the measure of all things." Indeed, value as we experience it is in what we offer to other people.

Recent findings suggest that stand far enough back and this is all one story. For all of history, humans did the work: with our muscles and with our minds. Twice, we built machines that took the work and externalized it to machines.

Industry observers note that the first time, we were terrified, and the fear was short-term justified and long-term wrong. The world after the machines took most of the physical work was profoundly more abundant, healthy  and humane.

The same trade is on the table now, at greater scale and higher speed. The Cognitive Revolution will be turbulent, unevenly distributed, and deeply uncomfortable . And, it will end the way the last one did: with the world unrecognizably better, its results so completely woven into daily life that our grandchildren will live inside them.

We have made this trip before.This time, we can navigate it with our eyes open: shaping the transition calmly, sharing the prosperity, and remembering that the goal of externalizing our minds is ultimately to elevate our humanity.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption. Cymphony is building the governance and security layer that removes it.

Controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption. Cymphony is building the governance and security layer that removes it.

In a recent development, every large enterprise now has an AI mandate. Very few know exactly what happens when an agent is granted access to enterprise systems and data. What exactly will it be able to reach? How will we know what it did with it? These questions â not model quality, not cost, not talent â are the reason so many enterprise AI programs stay stuck in pilots. Cymphony was built to answer them.

Employees increasingly work together with AI agents to execute day-to-day work. But the typical agent is nothing like an employee. It can be provisioned in minutes rather than hired over weeks. It works continuously. And it can reach across far more systems, data, and capability than an individual person. Every one of those properties is what makes an AI agent worth deploying â and every one of them is what makes a security team say no.

Governance and security are already major barriers to AI adoption, with 40% of enterprises expected to demote or decommission autonomous AI agents over governance concerns by next year. That is not a prediction about AI failing to work. Itâs about enterprises pulling back working agents because they cannot see or control what those agents reaching. The fundamental challenge is not utility, but accountability.

For decades, security teams have built tools around two separate concerns: where sensitive data lives, and who has access. The first produced the tools that watch files, inboxes, and databases for leaks. The second produced the identity industry. But both assume the "who"s are human employees.

Sources indicate that AI broke that assumption. An identity tool can tell you an agent exists. A data tool can tell you a file is sensitive. Neither can tell you that a given agent, acting on behalf of a given employee, can reach that file right now. Identity security and data security are no longer separable.

According to recent reports, cymphony continuously maps both employees and agents across an enterprise, graphing who and what can reach which systems and information. It is a difficult engineering problem: the same person routinely holds a dozen different accounts scattered across systems that were never designed to talk to each other, and agents inherit access from the humans and applications that spawned them. Stitching all of that back into one accurate picture requires more than a dashboard that aggregates alerts.

According to recent reports, what we love about working with co-founders Shy Dekel, Idan Berkovits, and Edi Gotlieb is their instinct to build not for the alert but for the workflow. Instead of stopping at detection and leaving a security analyst to figure out what to do next, Cymphony pushes further â recommending and even automating remediation, and coordinating with the people who need to take action.

Enterprise customers including Syngenta, KKR, Cass Information Systems, and Athennian are already seeing results. Sequoia is also a happy customer. We are proud to have led Cymphonyâs seed round, and to now co-lead their Series A.

Sources indicate that we met Shy, Idan, and Edi through Sequoia's Israel network, introduced separately by two people in our orbit who each said some version of the same thing: these three had spent their careers on hard, unglamorous security problem many founders avoid, and they were building something different around it. All three came out of Israel's elite Talpiot program. All three have deep experience in this space: Shy led the cyber department for Unit 8200, Idan ran a research group in the Office of the Prime Minister and won an Israel Defense Prize, and Edi built hardware at Apple and at the Israeli Ministry of Defense. Every large enterprise software tech giant has been built on a transition: the underlying unit of work changes, and the old categories are no longer the right shape. Cloud changed where software ran, and security rebuilt itself around it. Mobile changed what an endpoint was, and it rebuilt itself again. Each time, the companies that offered visibility and control over what came next eventually became infrastructure everyone else took for granted.

AI is no exception, albeit the first shift where the newly introduced unit of work can act on its own. The company that lets an enterprise say yes to agents â confidently, at scale, with a record of what they did â will be not just a feature inside the AI stack, but a precondition for it. We think Cymphony is building that layer, and we are glad to be part of it.

By Bogomil Balkansky, Dean Meyer and David Cahn.

In the digital era, this work still required painstakingly convincing customers to take online surveys; a meaningful study could take a full year. But market research is built almost entirely on language. Itâs about asking questions and listening to the answers. And LLMs are the best tool weâve ever had to do exactly that.

Less than a year after November 2022âs ChatGPT moment, Alfred and Florian identified a truly perfect market-technology fit for LLMs. What better way to be customer-obsessed than to hear directly from your customers not just once a year, but every month or even every week? While your competition waited a year for its next market research project to be processed, Listen Labsâ models and software could make customer studies real-time and continuous. ALFRED, FLORIAN AND BRYAN SIGNING THE TERM SHEET.

CHARLIE, BRYAN AND THE LISTEN LABS TEAM AT AN OFFSITE AT BRYANâS HOUSE.

Sail is building the inference stack and runtime for agents that work for hours, days and weeks. This is the token factory of the future.

Sail is building the inference stack and runtime for agents that work for hours, days and weeks. This is the token factory of the future.

Lauren and Konstantine with Neil and Samir.

Recent findings suggest that for years, "using AI" has mostly meant humans typing into a box and waiting for an answer. The next chapter belongs to agents. Machines chase solutions to any problem with patience and tenacity, bound only by the compute and context they are given.

In a recent development, the demand for agents is here. The infrastructure to run them ambitiously is not. Sail is the platform to run agents ambitiously.

It has been revealed that sail is building for a world in which agents run for hours or days to solve our most complex problems. Sail purpose-built their inference platform to operate across a wide range of compute and flex to handle long running, agent tasks. To make this happen, the Sail team is pushing on two key technologies:.

The first is their inference stack, the machinery that actually runs the models. Sail lives by a simple mantra, "there are no bad chips, only bad prices." The team took the inference stack apart and rebuilt it to squeeze far more out of every chip. They distribute work intelligently across providers so nothing stalls. They tap underused data-center capacity that would otherwise sit idle, particularly clusters too small or too old for anyone else to want. They're often among the first to try latest accelerators as they hit the market, always searching for a way to find a productive place for them in their engine.

This improved stack allows agents to think longer and harder, spending billions of tokens on a single task, for a fraction of the cost.

According to recent reports, the second is Sailboxes, the workspace for agents that want to run forever. Sailboxes fluidly scale CPU and memory to match the userâs needs, so an agent waiting on an event or long-running tool call is billed almost nothing for that time. Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

AI took the digital world by storm in a few short years, and we are still only scratching the surface. Each time digital AI has moved to a latest phase, from pretraining to reinforcement learning to deployment, spend on compute and data has not plateaued. It has accelerated.

Recent findings suggest that bringing AI into the physical world will be a wave of comparable importance to digital AI, if not larger, but the infrastructure required to get there will be harder to build and scale, and that already reveals at every stage. In pretraining, language models benefited from decades of text accumulated on the internet. Robotics has no comparable, ready-made collection of the movements, interactions and sensory information needed to understand the physical world. That experience has to be captured before it can be learned from. In reinforcement learning and deployment, digital AI operates in clean, structured environments that are easy to scale. Physical AI lives in the noisy, unpredictable, operationally complex reality of the real world. It operates in the field, not in the cloud.

To reach physical AGI, the industry has to build both the brain and the body. The brain needs data that wasnât collected. The body needs someone doing the work on the ground.

That is the mission Josh, Jason and the Mecka AI team have taken on: helping physical AI labs, robotics companies and end enterprises reach physical AGI and put it to use, by being their partner for training data, reinforcement learning, and deployment.

Delivering on this mission requires developing several muscles across disciplines, all at once and all at scale:.

Research: Identify the next wave in robotics, and what it will require, before it arrives.

Hardware: Once you see the wave, design the bespoke hardware and wearables to capture the data, then manufacture them fast, economically, and at scale.

It has been revealed that operations: Run large-scale global operations to collect the data. Volume alone is not enough; the data has to span every job in every industry.

Software and digital AI: Turn the raw output, which is far more voluminous and complex than text (e.g., multi-camera video, body and hand tracking, sensor streams), into high-quality, training-ready data.

Deployment: Put robots in front of end customers, for reinforcement learning and production deployment.

Each of these muscles is difficult to develop on its own, but to win, you need not one but all of them, working together and at scale. Training data today, for example, has to be high volume AND high diversity AND high quality AND delivered fast AND at a good price. It is easy to do one of these at small volume, but it is incredibly difficult to do all of them at once and at scale, and that is what it takes to help partners reach physical AGI. In the same way, it is easy to start a food delivery business that delivers a single dish from one restaurant to one apartment block, but it is incredibly difficult to scale it into a DoorDash.

Sources indicate that mecka's founders and team understood this and moved fast to build all five muscles, finding differentiated edge in each and executing on it. The result is a strong, scalable and flexible platform that has enabled them to win over many of the leading AI labs and robotics companies and rapidly become the emerging leader of this category.

Industry observers note that what drew us to Mecka is not that they made the right bet on the right form of data (although they did). Robotics is still early relative to digital AI. The form factor of the data might change. The form factor of the robots might change. What matters is that they built the machine that scales with the industry and its partners; regardless of how the input changes over time, the output will be what their partners want. In the same way, DoorDash built a system where, whether the input is a pizza or a laptop, the customer gets the same delightful delivery experience. And when something in the physical world has high barriers to scale, it is an opportunity for the right team to build a large, durable business with moats.

Recent findings suggest that that is why we are excited to back Josh, Jason and their fast-growing team. We see in them the special ingredients that will keep compounding over the long term to win this category and help their partners advance the mission of building and deploying robots at scale around the world.

And it is why others have joined us, from strategics like NVIDIA, Samsung, Microsoft and Qualcomm to the founders and operators who scaled some of the most defining companies of their generation and excel in many of the disciplines required in Meckaâs business: Tony Xu, founder and CEO of DoorDash; Frank Slootman, former CEO of ServiceNow and Snowflake; Milan Kovac, former head of Optimus at Tesla; Christopher Payne, former President & COO of Doordash; Jonathan Chadwick, former COO and CFO of VMware and board member at Databricks; and many more.Photo by S72 Business Portraits.

What if machine intelligence were as dependable as a database query?

What if machine intelligence were as dependable as a database query?

If models have reached superhuman intelligence, where is all the automation?

Industry observers note that the ChatGPT moment put AI front and center in the consumer mind. Claude Code transformed the life of the individual developer. With the âJev moment,â TypeSafe is going after the next paradigm: models that power software at runtime, making zillions of decisions with no humans in the loop.

Industry observers note that the early response has been extraordinary. Within 24 hours of launch on September 15, TypeSafeâs first model, Jev, became the fastest-adopted model in Vercelâs AI Gateway history. Over the past few weeks, weâve heard from many of our portfolio companies, who are racing to put it into production for a myriad of fresh use cases. It is the type of developer pull we havenât seen since GPT-3.

Recent findings suggest that jev flips the LLM on its head. Rather than writing out an answer word by word, it takes in context and a set of questions and returns typed answers with confidence scores, all at once. If LLMs are AIâs System 2, slow and deliberate, Jev is System 1: cheap, fast, intuitive and built for the thousands of small judgment calls software makes every second.

Industry observers note that thereâs so much you can do with Jev. Decide which button an agent should click next. Grade evals, route requests, triage tickets, pull fields out of contracts. Jev offers the kind of out-of-the-box generality that feels like magic, with no labeled data or training team required. Developers are finding newly introduced use cases every day, from playing Doom, to re-ranking their news feeds, to generating Super Mario multiverses.

According to recent reports, jev is named after Jevons paradox: when something gets dramatically cheaper, we use far more of it. TypeSafe is betting the same will be true of intelligence.

Industry observers note that when classification is expensive, teams ration it. They grade a sample of agent runs rather than all of them, define brittle rules instead of calling on a model, or ask one broad question instead of ten specific ones. When classification is nearly free, those tradeoffs go away.

That changes what is worth building. Many of the world's problems are Jev-shaped, which is obvious from the explosion of volume and creativity in use cases that folks are discovering. We think itâs likely that the most important things to be built on Jev havenât even been imagined yet.

Diogo Almeida first got the idea for TypeSafe while working on InstructGPT and RLHF at OpenAI. Models were being trained to be wonderful conversational partners â great for human interaction and human-in-the-loop. But, real automation needed something different: AI that is reliable, fast, and cheap. His conclusion, which he calls the âbitterest lesson,â was that picking the right task to solve matters even more than scale.

According to recent reports, born in the Philippines and a *top 30* North American League of Legends player, Diogo is a rare mix: an iconoclastic, creative researcher with real developer taste and commercial instinct. He is wildly ambitious and refreshingly pragmatic, which is exactly what is needed to usher in the next machine age.

Jev has captured lightning in a bottle, but it is only the opening salvo. TypeSafe wants to become the infrastructure layer for how software makes decisions: a platform of primitives developers can compose and build on, the way they once built on databases.

We are absolutely thrilled to be partnering with Diogo, co-founders Sasha Sheng and Erik Spock Gafni, and the TypeSafe team in their Series A, behind our friends at a16z.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip firm he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back.

According to recent reports, during the manufacturer’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering.

Sources indicate that “On November 12, our board of directors confirmed that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones noted, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”.

On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China, and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Industry observers note that the development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia. Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. Jones added Tuesday that the tech giant was looking at both internal and external candidates.

  • Sources indicate that “At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress stated in her opening remarks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company’s commitment to open source AI during Tuesday’s earnings call with analysts — the first since CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation.

Sources indicate that “At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress stated in her opening remarks. She also noted that open models were accelerating AI adoption, citing a 35-fold year-over-year surge in weekly token volume on OpenRouter, including a 3.5-fold increase over the past three months.

Kress also spoke about Nvidia’s looks for Hugging Face, a platform for open source AI models that the company agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September, in what would be the second-largest acquisition in Nvidia’s history.

Industry observers note that the platform, which serves more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, is still on track to join Nvidia, despite Huang’s ouster. Huang had heavily advocated for open source AI technology. His departure had raised questions about the company’s future approach to open source AI models, with Hugging Face’s CEO calling Huang’s departure “a sad day,” and promising to “keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever.”.

Industry observers note that so far, Nvidia’s prepares for Hugging Face appear unchanged. The acquisition was not directly addressed during the Q&A portion of the earnings call.

“Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable, and more accessible,” mentioned Kress of Nvidia’s prepares for Hugging Face.

Last week, Nvidia founder Huang resigned from his position as CEO following news about his extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based organization Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. He’s also accused of having extramarital affairs with two direct reports and is now set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. Meanwhile, the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, The WSJ reported.

Recent findings suggest that within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads. On today’s call, Kress noted that Nemotron is now the “most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter,” and it’s “where developers start to build their own intelligence.”.

“That foundation is empowering the ecosystem,” she noted.

Correction: Due to a typo, an earlier version of this article incorrectly stated the number of developers served by Hugging Face; it is 18 million, not 118 million.

Breaking: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S.
  • It has been revealed that china’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the organization’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week.
  • Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.

It has been revealed that china’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the organization’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia revealed it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks.

Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.

According to recent reports, the pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more crucial for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.”.

Sources indicate that huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.

According to recent reports, investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress noted that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue.

In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change.

Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute consumers want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.

Sources indicate that that training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.

If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share.

JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.

JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.

Recent findings suggest that software development has a new bottleneck. Writing code is no longer the hard part; trusting it is. Coding agents now produce more code than any team can read or any existing system can verify. Led by co-founders Aditya Jayaprakash (JP), Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, Blacksmith is building infrastructure that can.

Recent findings suggest that last month, Anthropicâs engineering team described what happened as their own usage of coding agents scaled. Engineers began shipping roughly eight times as much code per quarter. Their test suite grew tenfold. The volume of continuous integration (CI) jobs, the builds and tests that check every change before it reaches production, grew 25x in six months. Anthropic is very far along the curve, but is on the same curve as every manufacturer, and its advice to the rest of the industry was to proposal for 25x the CI load within two quarters.

It has been revealed that for decades, software development scaled as a function of engineering capacity. Developers were the scarce resource. Shipping more meant hiring more. That has changed. Developers now direct fleets of coding agents that work in parallel, around the clock and increasingly autonomously. These agents do not produce finished work. They produce attemptsâa patch, a test, a migration, a throwaway branchâeach iterating against a test suite until it is ready to merge. Meanwhile, the quiet backbone of software development that validates and tests code has not changed.

Industry observers note that validating code has also never been more crucial. AI coding tasks produce large volumes of security flaws, and the same model capabilities that write the code now make those flaws more dangerous. The system that was supposed to catch them is straining right as developers need it the most. With the scale and velocity of this shift, the constraint in software has moved from writing code to proving it works and is safe.

Recent findings suggest that this is the problem Blacksmith set out to solve. The team started with speeding up CI. With a one-line change in a workflow file, developers using Blacksmith see their CI jobs complete twice as fast and at 60% lower cost on average. Underneath a simple product experience is a stack purpose-built from the bare metal up, designed to absorb demand spikes from customers and get faster and more efficient as it scales.

Developers have noticed. The business has seen explosive growth this year. More than 10,000 companies are using Blacksmith, up from 700 a year ago. Weekly CI jobs are up 18x, from 5 million to 90 million, in 2026 alone. And ARR has grown 17x over the same time period, with the largest customers now spending more than $1M per year.

Much of our conviction in Blacksmith is driven by the team behind it. Co-founders JP, Aayush and Maru have known each other since their undergraduate years at the University of Waterloo, and developed a maniacal focus on hyper-performant systems at Cockroach Labs and Faire. They founded Blacksmith in 2024, as autocomplete was giving way to coding assistants, on the conviction that the volume of code needing to be tested would go up by orders of magnitude. For the rest of the world, the future became clear in 2026 with the arrival of truly autonomous coding agents, but Blacksmith had already been building for it. The Blacksmith team is talent-dense and is growing quickly. The roadmap is exciting, with several rolls out planned in the coming months.

We are proud to lead Blacksmithâs Series C. The world is about to run far more code than it has ever written, and someone has to make sure it works. We look forward to supporting JP, Aayush and Maru as they build infrastructure that runs at agent speed, in validation and beyond.

  • Yet, there’s still more that the VC firm founded by Skype’s Niklas Zennström would like to see — and its call this year is for Europe to “build it” and “scale it,” but also “own it.” That’s a way of wishing these companies will remain European longer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Europe is home to many of the world’s fastest growing companies of all time, veteran VC firm Atomico highlighted in its latest annual State of European Tech report.

Industry observers note that the report, for instance, notes that the likes of Black Forest Labs and Microagi have reached $100 million in revenue in months, not years. “I think we can put to bed the idea that there’s a fundamental reason or constraint on the ability to scale a breakout company from here in Europe,” Atomico partner and head of intelligence Tom Wehmeier (pictured) told TechCrunch.

Yet, there’s still more that the VC firm founded by Skype’s Niklas Zennström would like to see — and its call this year is for Europe to “build it” and “scale it,” but also “own it.” That’s a way of wishing these companies will remain European longer. But there’s also a sense that this success hasn’t been acknowledged enough, perhaps obscured by louder calls for improvements.

Wehmeier, the report’s lead author, was quick to opine that “policy, procurement and capital are not moving at the same speed as our founders.” But he said the tech sector should advocate for itself in an inspiring way.

Industry observers note that “When it comes to policy, I think the language needs to be, ‘Hey, this is not us complaining. This is us saying here is an opportunity to make the magnitude of impact even greater,’” Wehmeier noted. “When we frame it as problems, that becomes harder.”.

This reframing may also help European tech improve its image abroad, where complaints around overregulation may have overshadowed Europe’s potential to leverage its deep tech talent and growing pool of repeat entrepreneurs to have even more of success stories.

Plenty could be still done to fully unlock this potential, and Wehmeier said that “the next few weeks are going to be a really crucial test, with EU Inc.” Also known as the 28th regime, this initiative would create a unified European corporate regime akin to the Delaware C Corp.

Sources indicate that if the last stretch of EU Inc’s grassroots campaign achieves it goal, it will become much easier to create and operate businesses across the EU. It would also show that the tech system got itself heard, which could open the door to the kind of endorsement Atomico is hoping to see more of.

In a recent development, politicians have strong incentives to give the tech sector what it wants. If it is Europe’s second largest sector, biggest contributor to growth, and biggest job creator, “Do we not want more of that?” Wehmeier asked rhetorically. But it is unclear whether it will win them any votes.

Sources indicate that to make the answer more straightforward, the tech sector will have to work on having public opinion on its side. For Wehmeier, one key is to “demonstrate that this is translating into value for citizens.”.

The report is supporting this endeavor with a mix of high-level data and examples from its portfolio; for instance, it notes that ICEYE’s satellites monitor severe weather, flooding, and other hazards; and Daniel Ek’s Neko Health has now done more than 100,000 body scans, some of which helped identify severe or life-threatening health conditions.

According to recent reports, one limit to this argument is that Neko Health’s scans will seem pricey to most Europeans, who largely rely on collective, public health insurance. But Atomico seems to hope that its report will give readers FOMO not just as potential customers, but also as potential shareholders.

Recent findings suggest that there’s more to be done for this to happen. Beyond joining the sector’s push for an EU capital markets union, he hopes more of Europe’s institutional investors will invest in the region’s own tech companies. “We must get to the place where Europe and European beneficiaries are the biggest shareholders in the success that we create,” Wehmeier stated.

It has been revealed that before that can happen, the industry must overcome anti-industry beliefs like fears of AI-induced job destruction. But Wehmeier is a believer in the power of proof. “I think that trust is going to be earned through showing results to the public — be that lower energy bills, better healthcare, more homes built for cheaper and faster, and having infrastructure that we can rely on.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that despite the turmoil at Nvidia following the departure of its disgraced founder and CEO Jensen Huang, the company — as expected — delivered a solid quarter on Tuesday. More importantly, Nvidia reassured investors that its streak of record-breaking revenue won’t stop.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim CEO Colette Kress reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from the year-ago quarter and a beat above the firm’s guidance. Nvidia had told Wall Street to expect $108 billion in revenue for its third quarter of fiscal 2027. Kress also projected an even bigger fourth quarter, with revenue expected to reach $130 billion, plus or minus 3%.

She also stated full-year revenue is on track to exceed expectations.

“We are raising our fiscal year 2028 outlook. We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% and off what is now a higher fiscal 2027 base,” Kress remarked on the quarterly conference call on Tuesday. “Our outlook considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.”.

Recent findings suggest that the company also reminded investors that it was using some of its billions in cash to buy back shares. In September 2026, Nvidia increased its share buyback program by $150 billion. It spent $28.1 billion on its own shares during the quarter and still had another $227.3 billion remaining in the kitty for additional repurchases.

In a recent development, ironically, Nvidia could also benefit from the plunge in its share price following Huang’s resignation last week, should shares remain depressed over the longer term. The stock is down about 10% since his departure. Investors, however, celebrated Tuesday’s quarterly results, sending shares up about 4% in after-hours trading.

Kress stressed that the firm was in good shape now and for the foreseeable future, even without Huang at the helm.

“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress stressed. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.”.

She added that the firm has secured memory and advanced packaging capacity and is working with its chip manufacturer, TSMC, to “narrow the supply and demand gaps.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: It revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both fresh investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies.

It has been revealed that the tech giant invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it noted, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year.

But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.

It has been revealed that nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.”  Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications.

It’s also become a major financier of the data center build-out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio.

Recent findings suggest that the company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earnings call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”.

But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm.

Industry observers note that huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies.

Recent findings suggest that “We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.

#5152. Industry News: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (960 w)

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years.
  • According to recent reports, graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge.
  • Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the firm exclusively told TechCrunch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite.

According to recent reports, graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries, is working to break that dominance.

Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the firm exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market.

Industry observers note that “The latest plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He remarked future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology.

In a recent development, molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells.

The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, noted Boyd.

Sources indicate that the startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage. It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd remarked. The manufacturer claims the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S.

“We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” remarked Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the firm’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.”.

In a recent development, here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements.

It has been revealed that the basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd said no manufacturer before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way.

Recent findings suggest that solving that problem changed the firm’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a by-product.

But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high-quality graphite,” Boyd mentioned, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen.

Sources indicate that the tech giant states both businesses could bring in billions of dollars. If Molten supplied the entire U.S. battery market, it could also provide about a third of the hydrogen used in the country, the company claims. Other uses for high-quality graphite, like thermal batteries that store energy as heat, could expand both markets further.

The latest factory, Boyd mentioned, “is really a milestone, not just for the company, we think, but globally.”.
